M1 Analog Modulation
25EC2205E · Modern Communication Systems · Module M1 · maps to CO1

Analog Modulation: start with the live system, then sixteen lectures and the labs

From "why modulate?" to hearing a real FM station through your own GNU Radio flowgraph. Lectures 1–11 teach the theory with derivations, interactive labs, solved numericals, practice and quizzes. Lectures 12–16 hold the circuit handbook, the GNU Radio labs, the Python and MATLAB programs with calculators, the quiz, assignments and PBL, and the syllabus map with references. The LABS tab holds every practical and skilling experiment, and the complete M2 and M3 module pages.

Eight topics, one story: a radio link followed from the microphone to the speaker. Each row opens its lecture.

#TopicWhat you will learnGo to
L1The need for modulationFrequency translation for transmission, multiplexing, antenna sizing
L2Amplitude Modulation (AM)The canonical \(s(t)=[A_c+m(t)]\cos\omega_ct\); modulation index, sideband structure
L3AM demodulationEnvelope detector, synchronous demodulation; noise performance
L4Frequency Modulation (FM)Instantaneous frequency, modulation index, Carson’s rule for bandwidth
L5FM demodulationDiscriminator, PLL-based demodulation; the noise-suppression advantage
L6Phase Modulation (PM)FM’s twin, one integrator apart, and the doorway to digital
L7Real-world contextsAM broadcast (520–1710 kHz in the Americas; 531–1602 kHz in India), FM broadcast (88–108 MHz), aviation VHF

The question to keep in mindYour phone (≈ 0.7–3.5 GHz), the FM radio in an auto-rickshaw (88–108 MHz) and the pilot talking to the tower (118–137 MHz, AM) all send voice through the air at the same time. How do they not mix? Every row above is part of the answer: each user gets its own carrier.

InteractiveCommunication System Live

Use ▶ Guided tour for a walk through every test point, or choose a modulation and change μ, Δf, kₚ, the receiver phase error, channel attenuation and SNR. Digital modes (ASK, BPSK, FSK) preview the next module.

GNU RadioThe same end-to-end system as one GNU Radio flowgraph

Every block of the live system above is built here in GNU Radio Companion 3.10: message, carrier, four modulators, channel, receiver band-pass, local oscillator, four detectors and the output filter. A Modulation chooser switches between AM, DSB-SC, FM and PM, and sliders change fm, fc, μ, Δf, kp, φ, α and the SNR, just like the page above. Each test point TP1–TP9 has a block named after it.

Animated flowgraph: every block, live

The same 64 blocks, laid out exactly as in the GRC editor, but now each block shows a live mini oscilloscope of its own output and dots flow along the wires in the direction the samples travel. The signals are computed in your browser with the same mathematics as the GNU Radio blocks. Click any block to see its input (blue/green) and output (red) together, the spectrum of its output, its parameters and why it is used. Guided tour walks through the blocks in signal-flow order. Grey boxes are variables and sliders; their current value is shown.

Click any block. Orange wires carry real (float) samples, teal wires complex samples.

Parameters:

How to read a GNU Radio flowgraph start here
  • Blocks and arrows. Each block does one job (generate, multiply, filter, display); arrows carry streams of samples from left to right. A flowgraph is a block diagram that actually runs.
  • Port colours = data type. Orange ports carry float (real) samples; blue ports carry complex (I + jQ) samples. Connected ports must have the same type, which is why some blocks have an “IO Type” or “Output Type” setting.
  • Variables and GUI blocks (Variable, QT GUI Range, QT GUI Chooser) have no ports. They hold numbers that other blocks use, and the GUI ones become sliders and drop-downs when the flowgraph runs.
  • Sources start the stream (Signal Source, Noise Source); sinks end it (Time Sink = oscilloscope, Frequency Sink = spectrum analyser, Audio Sink = loudspeaker).
  • Sample rate. Every block works on samples, so every block must agree on samp_rate; it must exceed twice the highest frequency in the system.
  • Throttle. A simulation with no hardware needs exactly one Throttle (or an Audio Sink) to run at real time; hardware sources and sinks set the pace themselves.
  • Choosing a block. Ask what the textbook block diagram does at that point, then find the GNU Radio block that does the same mathematics: product modulator → Multiply, envelope detector → Abs + low-pass, FM discriminator → Quadrature Demod. The “Why this block” column below gives this reasoning for every block.

Test points and the blocks that make them

TPSignalGNU Radio blocksBlock IDWhy it is needed
TP1Message m(t): one tone fm, or fm + 3fmSignal Source ×2 → AddTP1_messageThe reference signal. Everything is judged by how closely TP9 matches it.
TP2Carrier cos 2πf꜀tSignal Source (float, f꜀)TP2_carrierA carrier is needed to move the message to a frequency an antenna can radiate and that other users do not share.
TP3Modulated signal s(t): AM, DSB-SC, FM or PMfour modulator branches → weighted Add (the Modulation chooser picks one)TP3_modulatedThis is what is actually transmitted; its shape and spectrum define the modulation.
TP4Channel noise n(t), σ set from the SNR in B_TNoise Source (Gaussian)TP4_noiseEvery real receiver adds noise; modelling it shows which modulation copes best.
TP5Received r(t) = α·s(t) + n(t)Multiply Const α → Add → ThrottleTP5_receivedWhat the receiver really gets: weak and noisy. All receiver blocks exist to clean this up.
TP6After the receiver band-pass, f꜀ ± B_T/2Band Pass FilterTP6_rx_bandpassSelects the wanted channel and removes out-of-band noise before detection.
TP7Local oscillator 2cos(2πf꜀t + φ)Signal Source (amplitude 2, phase φ)TP7_local_oscCoherent detectors need a copy of the carrier; its phase error shows why synchronisation matters.
TP8Detector output: envelope (AM), product (DSB-SC), discriminator (FM), phase (PM)Abs · Multiply · Quadrature Demod · Complex to Arg → weighted AddTP8_detectorConverts the carrier variation (amplitude, phase or frequency) back into a voltage proportional to m(t).
TP9Recovered message m̂(t)Low Pass Filter → DC BlockerTP9_recoveredRemoves leftover carrier terms, noise and DC: the final output to compare with TP1.

What you see when it runs (F6)

Top left of each window: TP1 message (blue) and TP9 recovered (red). The red trace lags because the band-pass and low-pass filters delay the signal (about 1–8 ms). Top right: TP3 transmitted and TP5 received. Bottom: spectra of TP3, TP5 and TP6, and the TP8 detector output.

Verified run

The flowgraph was compiled with GNU Radio 3.10 and run for every modulation at a channel SNR of 30 dB, with one tone and with two tones. TP9 was compared with TP1 after removing the filter delay.

ModulationDetectorTP9 / TP1 amplitudeOutput SNR, one tone / two tones (dB)
AMenvelope (Abs + LPF)0.95–0.9923.6 / 24.9
DSB-SCcoherent product, φ = 00.96–1.0031.8 / 32.2
FMquadrature discriminator0.96–0.9943.4 / 30.8

Build and run it

  1. Install GNU Radio 3.10 (Radioconda on Windows/macOS, or sudo apt install gnuradio on Ubuntu).
  2. Copy the flowgraph text below into a file named m1_comm_system.grc, or build it yourself from the block table and the connection list.
  3. Open it in GNU Radio Companion, press F5 to generate and F6 to run. No SDR hardware is needed.
  4. Try the same experiments as the live page: raise μ above 1 in AM; set φ = 90° in DSB-SC; lower the SNR to 0 dB and compare AM with FM; switch to two tones and watch the spectrum.
All 64 blocks: parameters to enter and why each block is used
#Block (Ctrl+F)Why this blockLibraryIDParameters
1VariableSets how many samples per second every block processes (200 kS/s). It must be more than twice the highest frequency in the system (carrier 20 kHz + FM sidebands), or the signals alias. All filters and sources read it.Variablessamp_rateValue 200e3
2QT GUI ChooserA drop-down that picks AM, DSB-SC, FM or PM while the flowgraph runs. One flowgraph then teaches all four modulations, and students can compare them on the same scopes.GUI Widgets ▸ QTmodLabel "Modulation" · Type int · Num Options 4 · Default option 0 · Label 0 "AM" · Label 1 "DSB-SC" · Label 2 "FM" · Label 3 "PM"
3QT GUI ChooserSwitches the message between one tone and two tones. Two tones show how a richer message widens the spectrum and how each modulation treats several frequencies at once.GUI Widgets ▸ QTtwoLabel "Message" · Type int · Num Options 2 · Default option 0 · Label 0 "Single tone" · Label 1 "Two tones (fm and 3fm)"
4QT GUI RangeSlider for the message frequency fm. Moving it shows that sidebands move with fm and that the bandwidth (2fm for AM, Carson for FM) depends on it.GUI Widgets ▸ QTfmLabel "Message frequency fm (Hz)" · Default Value 1000 · Start 250 · Stop 3000 · Step 250
5QT GUI RangeSlider for the carrier frequency fc. It shows frequency translation: the whole spectrum shifts with fc, while the recovered message stays the same.GUI Widgets ▸ QTfcLabel "Carrier frequency fc (Hz)" · Default Value 10000 · Start 6000 · Stop 20000 · Step 500
6QT GUI RangeSlider for the AM modulation index μ. Above μ = 1 the envelope crosses zero and the envelope detector output distorts: over-modulation seen live.GUI Widgets ▸ QTmuLabel "AM index mu" · Default Value 0.6 · Start 0.1 · Stop 1.5 · Step 0.05
7QT GUI RangeSlider for the FM peak deviation Δf. Larger Δf widens the FM spectrum (Carson’s rule) and improves the output SNR: the FM bandwidth-for-noise trade.GUI Widgets ▸ QTdfLabel "FM deviation df (Hz)" · Default Value 2500 · Start 250 · Stop 5000 · Step 250
8QT GUI RangeSlider for the PM sensitivity kp in radians. Shows how phase deviation sets the PM bandwidth and the detector output level.GUI Widgets ▸ QTkpLabel "PM sensitivity kp (rad)" · Default Value 1.5 · Start 0.2 · Stop 2.5 · Step 0.1
9QT GUI RangeSlider for the receiver local-oscillator phase error φ. For DSB-SC the output falls as cos φ and vanishes at 90°: why coherent receivers need carrier recovery.GUI Widgets ▸ QTphiLabel "LO phase error phi (deg)" · Default Value 0 · Stop 90 · Step 5
10QT GUI RangeSlider for channel attenuation α (path loss). The received signal shrinks while the noise does not, so the SNR falls: the real reason long links fail.GUI Widgets ▸ QTalphaLabel "Channel attenuation alpha" · Default Value 0.5 · Start 0.1 · Stop 1 · Step 0.05
11QT GUI RangeSlider for the channel SNR measured in the transmission bandwidth BT. It sets the noise level so every modulation is compared at the same SNR, a fair comparison.GUI Widgets ▸ QTsnrLabel "Channel SNR in B_T (dB)" · Default Value 20 · Start -5 · Stop 40
12VariableHighest message frequency W: fm for one tone, 3fm for two tones. Filters and bandwidth formulas use it.VariablesfmaxValue fm*(3 if two else 1)
13VariableAverage message power Pm. Needed to compute the transmitted power and set the correct noise level for the chosen SNR.VariablesPmValue 0.5*(1 + 0.25*two)
14VariableTransmission bandwidth BT of the chosen modulation: 2W for AM and DSB-SC, Carson’s rule 2(Δf + W) for FM and PM. The receiver band-pass filter is sized from it.VariablesBTValue [2*fmax, 2*fmax, 2*(df + fmax), 2*(kp + 1)*fmax][mod]
15VariableAverage power of the modulated signal for the chosen modulation, used to turn the SNR slider into a noise amplitude.VariablesPsValue [(1 + mu**2*Pm)/2, Pm/2, 0.5, 0.5][mod]
16VariableNoise standard deviation computed from α, the signal power, BT and the SNR slider. It turns the SNR you ask for into the actual noise amplitude of the Noise Source.VariablessigmaValue alpha*(Ps*(samp_rate/2)/(BT*10**(snr/10)))**0.5
17VariableNumber of taps of the receiver band-pass filter (always odd). More taps give a sharper filter but more delay; the value is tied to fm so the filter stays sharp enough.VariablesnbpValue int(53*samp_rate/(22.0*fm))//2*2 + 1
18VariableTotal delay (in samples) of the band-pass filter and the Hilbert transformer. The FM/PM receiver uses it to correct the local-oscillator phase so the phase detector reads the right value.Variablesrx_delayValue (nbp - 1)/2 + 64
19VariableList of four weights, one of them 1 and the rest 0. It switches on only the modulator chosen in the drop-down. GNU Radio has no simple switch block, so weighted adding is the cleanest way.Variablesw_txValue [1.0*(mod == k) for k in range(4)]
20VariableFour receiver weights: they pick the matching detector and also scale its output (1/α, 1/kp, …) so the recovered message has the same size as the original.Variablesw_rxValue [3.14159/(2*alpha*mu)*(mod == 0), (mod == 1)/alpha, 1.0*(mod == 2), (mod == 3)/kp]
21Signal SourceGenerates the message tone cos 2πfmt. Signal Source is the standard GNU Radio oscillator; a pure tone makes every spectrum line easy to identify.Waveform Generatorstone1Output Type float · Frequency fm
22Signal SourceSecond message tone at 3fm, switched on by the “Two tones” option (amplitude 0 otherwise). It makes the message more like real audio.Waveform Generatorstone2Output Type float · Frequency 3*fm · Amplitude 0.5*two
23AddAdds the two tones to form the message m(t). Test point TP1: the reference that the recovered message TP9 is compared with.Math OperatorsTP1_messageIO Type float
24Signal SourceGenerates the carrier cos 2πfct (TP2). Every modulator needs a high-frequency carrier to move the message up in frequency.Waveform GeneratorsTP2_carrierOutput Type float · Frequency fc
25Multiply ConstMultiplies the message by μ. This scales how deeply the message changes the carrier amplitude: the definition of the modulation index.Math Operatorsam_indexIO Type float · Constant mu
26Add ConstAdds 1 to give 1 + μm(t). This is what puts the carrier into AM (DSB-FC), so the envelope stays positive and a simple envelope detector works.Math Operatorsam_plus_oneIO Type float · Constant 1
27MultiplyMultiplies [1 + μm(t)] by the carrier: the AM equation s(t) = Ac[1 + μm(t)] cos ωct. A product block is the textbook product modulator.Math Operatorsam_modulatorIO Type float
28MultiplyMultiplies m(t) directly by the carrier: DSB-SC with no carrier component. Comparing it with AM shows the power saved and why coherent detection becomes necessary.Math Operatorsdsb_modulatorIO Type float
29Multiply ConstMultiplies m(t) by Δf, turning the message into a frequency offset in hertz: Δf·m(t).Math Operatorsfm_deviationIO Type float · Constant df
30Add ConstAdds fc so the instantaneous frequency is fc + Δf·m(t): the definition of FM.Math Operatorsfm_plus_fcIO Type float · Constant fc
31VCOVoltage-controlled oscillator: its output frequency follows its input. Feeding it fc + Δf·m(t) produces FM directly, exactly like a hardware VCO-based FM transmitter.Waveform Generatorsfm_vcoSample Rate samp_rate · Sensitivity 2*3.14159265 · Amplitude 1
32Phase ModPhase Mod outputs ejkpm(t): a complex baseband signal whose phase follows the message. This is PM at baseband.Modulatorspm_modulatorSensitivity kp
33Signal SourceComplex carrier ej2πfct used to move the baseband PM signal up to fc.Waveform Generatorspm_carrierOutput Type complex · Frequency fc
34MultiplyMultiplies the PM baseband by the complex carrier: frequency translation from 0 Hz to fc, the same job a mixer does in a radio.Math Operatorspm_upconvertIO Type complex
35Complex To RealKeeps the real part, cos[ωct + kpm(t)]: the real signal an antenna would actually radiate.Type Converterspm_realdefaults
36Multiply ConstWeight w_tx[0]: passes the AM branch only when AM is selected.Math Operatorstx_select_0IO Type float · Constant w_tx[0]
37Multiply ConstWeight w_tx[1]: passes the DSB-SC branch only when DSB-SC is selected.Math Operatorstx_select_1IO Type float · Constant w_tx[1]
38Multiply ConstWeight w_tx[2]: passes the FM branch only when FM is selected.Math Operatorstx_select_2IO Type float · Constant w_tx[2]
39Multiply ConstWeight w_tx[3]: passes the PM branch only when PM is selected.Math Operatorstx_select_3IO Type float · Constant w_tx[3]
40AddAdds the four weighted branches; only the selected one is non-zero, so the output is the chosen modulated signal s(t), test point TP3.Math OperatorsTP3_modulatedIO Type float · Num Inputs 4
41Multiply ConstMultiplies s(t) by α: path loss in the channel. Real signals arrive millions of times weaker than they were sent.Math Operatorschannel_alphaIO Type float · Constant alpha
42Noise SourceGaussian noise n(t) (TP4), with amplitude σ from the SNR slider. Thermal noise in receivers is Gaussian, so this is the standard AWGN channel model.Waveform GeneratorsTP4_noiseOutput Type float · Amplitude sigma · Seed 42
43AddAdds the attenuated signal and the noise: r(t) = α·s(t) + n(t), the received signal at TP5.Math OperatorsTP5_receivedIO Type float
44ThrottleLimits the flowgraph to samp_rate samples per second. With no hardware (no SDR, no sound card) the computer would otherwise run flat out and freeze the scopes. Needed in every simulation-only flowgraph, exactly once.Miscblocks_throttle2_0Type float
45Band Pass FilterReceiver band-pass filter centred on fc with width BT (TP6). It keeps the wanted station and removes noise outside its band: the job of the tuned RF stage in a radio.FiltersTP6_rx_bandpassFIR Type fir_filter_fff · Low Cutoff Freq max(fc - BT/2 - fm, 300) · High Cutoff Freq fc + BT/2 + fm · Transition Width fm
46Signal SourceLocal oscillator 2cos(2πfct + φ) (TP7) for coherent detection. The factor 2 makes the product detector return m(t) at full size; φ lets you test phase errors.Waveform GeneratorsTP7_local_oscOutput Type float · Frequency fc · Amplitude 2 · Initial Phase (Radians) phi*3.14159265/180
47AbsAbsolute value = an ideal diode rectifier. Followed by the low-pass filter it forms the envelope detector for AM: simple, cheap and needs no local oscillator.Math Operatorsam_envelopeIO Type float
48MultiplyMultiplies the received signal by the local oscillator: the product (coherent) detector for DSB-SC. The low-pass filter after it removes the 2fc term.Math Operatorsdsb_productIO Type float
49HilbertHilbert transformer: turns the real received signal into a complex (analytic) signal with I and Q parts. FM and PM detectors need I and Q to measure phase and frequency.Filtersrx_hilbertNum Taps 129
50Signal SourceComplex local oscillator e−j2πfct with its phase corrected for the filter delay. It moves the analytic signal down to 0 Hz (baseband).Waveform Generatorsrx_complex_loOutput Type complex · Frequency -fc · Initial Phase (Radians) 2*3.14159265*fc*rx_delay/samp_rate
51MultiplyMultiplies by the complex LO: shifts the signal from fc to baseband, where its phase is kpm(t) (PM) or its frequency is Δf·m(t) (FM).Math Operatorsrx_to_basebandIO Type complex
52Quadrature DemodQuadrature Demod measures the change of phase between samples = instantaneous frequency. With gain fs/(2πΔf) the output is m(t). This is GNU Radio’s standard FM discriminator, used in every FM receiver flowgraph.Modulatorsfm_discriminatorGain samp_rate/(2*3.14159265*df)
53Complex to ArgComplex to Arg gives the phase angle of each sample. For PM that phase is kpm(t), so this block is the phase detector.Type Converterspm_phase_detectordefaults
54Multiply ConstWeight w_rx[0]: passes and scales the envelope-detector output when AM is selected.Math Operatorsrx_select_0IO Type float · Constant w_rx[0]
55Multiply ConstWeight w_rx[1]: passes and scales the product-detector output when DSB-SC is selected.Math Operatorsrx_select_1IO Type float · Constant w_rx[1]
56Multiply ConstWeight w_rx[2]: passes the discriminator output when FM is selected.Math Operatorsrx_select_2IO Type float · Constant w_rx[2]
57Multiply ConstWeight w_rx[3]: passes the phase-detector output (÷ kp) when PM is selected.Math Operatorsrx_select_3IO Type float · Constant w_rx[3]
58AddAdds the four weighted detector outputs; only the selected detector is non-zero. Test point TP8: the raw detector output before filtering.Math OperatorsTP8_detectorIO Type float · Num Inputs 4
59Low Pass FilterLow-pass filter at 1.5 × W. It removes the carrier ripple and 2fc terms and the out-of-band noise left by the detector, leaving only the message band.Filtersrx_lowpassFIR Type fir_filter_fff · Cutoff Freq 1.5*fmax · Transition Width fm
60DC BlockerDC Blocker removes the constant (DC) level, e.g. the carrier term in AM. Its output is the recovered message m̂(t), test point TP9.FiltersTP9_recoveredType ff · Length 2048
61QT GUI Time SinkOscilloscope with TP1 and TP9 overlaid: the single most important check that the system works. The output should look like the input, delayed by the filters.Instrumentation ▸ QTscope_messageType float · Name "TP1 message (blue) and TP9 recovered (red)" · Number of Points 2000 · Grid True · Y min -2 · Y max 2 · Number of Inputs 2 · Line 1 Label "TP1 message" · Line 2 Label "TP9 recovered"
62QT GUI Time SinkOscilloscope with TP3 (sent) and TP5 (received): shows the effect of path loss and noise on the modulated waveform.Instrumentation ▸ QTscope_signalType float · Name "TP3 transmitted (blue) and TP5 received (red)" · Number of Points 2000 · Grid True · Y min -2 · Y max 2 · Number of Inputs 2 · Line 1 Label "TP3 transmitted" · Line 2 Label "TP5 received"
63QT GUI Frequency SinkSpectrum analyser for TP3, TP5 and TP6: shows the sidebands, the bandwidth BT, the noise floor and how the band-pass filter cleans the received signal.Instrumentation ▸ QTspectrumType float · Name "Spectra: TP3 transmitted, TP5 received, TP6 after band-pass" · FFT Size 4096 · Grid True · Average 0.2 · Y min -100 · Number of Inputs 3 · Line 1 Label "TP3" · Line 2 Label "TP5" · Line 3 Label "TP6"
64QT GUI Time SinkOscilloscope on TP8: shows what the detector produces before low-pass filtering (rectified carrier for AM, double-frequency terms for DSB-SC).Instrumentation ▸ QTscope_detectorType float · Name "TP8 detector output (before low-pass)" · Number of Points 2000 · Grid True · Autoscale True · Y min -3 · Y max 3

metadata:
    file_format: 1
    grc_version: 3.10.9.2

AnimatedDigital communication systems, block by block

The complete digital link as drawn in Sklar's Digital Communications: the transmitter chain on top, the channel on the right, the receiver chain underneath. Hatched blocks are optional, plain blocks are essential. The signal names on the diagram (mᵢ, uᵢ, gᵢ(t), sᵢ(t), h_c(t), r(t), z(T), ûᵢ, m̂ᵢ) light up as the signal passes them. Press Play, or click any block.

AnimatedAnalog communication system: the waveform at every block

Every block shows two live mini-scopes: IN, the signal entering it, and OUT, the signal leaving it. The arrows carry the signal; the glowing pulse walks through the system one block at a time and the large scopes below zoom in on that block. Click any block to stop on it.

INPUT
OUTPUT

GNU RadioThe waveform at every block, in GNU Radio

The animated diagram above, built as a GNU Radio Companion 3.10 flowgraph. Each of the 12 blocks of the transmitter, channel and receiver is a GNU Radio block (or a short chain of blocks), and each has its own scope showing the signal going IN (blue) and coming OUT (red). You hear the recovered message on the loudspeaker.

New to flowgraphs? The guide “How to read a GNU Radio flowgraph” is in the section above.

Each block of the diagram and its GNU Radio blocks

#Diagram blockGNU Radio blocksOutput IDWaveform at its outputWhy it is needed
1Information sourceTwo Signal Sources (500 Hz, 1200 Hz) → Addsrc_soundspeech-like sound p(t)Every communication starts with information to send (voice, music, data).
2Input transducerMultiply Const 0.003 (microphone)micm(t), a few millivoltsElectronics handle voltages, not sound, so a transducer converts the sound into an electrical signal.
3AmplifierMultiply Const ≈ 333audio_ampm(t), about 1 VThe microphone signal is too small for a modulator; amplification brings it to a usable level.
4ModulatorMultiply Const μ → Add Const 1 → Multiply by carrier (Signal Source f꜀)am_modulatorA꜀[1 + μm(t)] cos ω꜀tLow-frequency audio cannot be radiated efficiently or shared between stations; modulation moves it onto a high-frequency carrier.
5Transmitting antennaMultiply Const 1 (RF power amplifier + antenna)tx_antennaradiated AM waveConverts the electrical signal into a radio wave that travels through space.
6ChannelMultiply Const α (path loss) → Addchannelweak AM + noiseThe medium between transmitter and receiver: it weakens the signal (path loss).
7NoiseNoise Source (Gaussian, slider)noisen(t)Noise is unavoidable; including it shows how the receiver must fight it.
8Receiving antennaBand Pass Filter f꜀ ± 3.5 kHz (tuned RF stage)rx_antenna_rfwanted station onlyPicks up the wave and selects one station, rejecting other stations and out-of-band noise.
9DemodulatorAbs (diode) → Single Pole IIR (RC)demodulatorenvelope: DC + message + rippleExtracts the message from the carrier: for AM, the envelope.
10DetectorLow Pass Filter 3.4 kHz → DC Blockerdetectorm̂(t), ripple and DC removedCleans the demodulated signal: removes carrier ripple, high-frequency noise and the DC level.
11AmplifierMultiply Const 1/(0.55αμ)power_ampamplified m̂(t)Raises the recovered message to a level that can drive a loudspeaker.
12Output transducer + destinationMultiply Const (volume) → Audio Sinkloudspeakersound you hearTurns the electrical signal back into sound for the listener.

Animated flowgraph: every block, live

All 41 blocks of this flowgraph at their GRC positions, each with a live mini oscilloscope of its output; the scope blocks show what their own window displays. Click any block for its input and output together, its spectrum and why it is there, or press Guided tour to follow the signal from the information source to the loudspeaker.

Click any block. Orange wires carry real (float) samples, teal wires complex samples.

Parameters:

Verified run

Compiled and run with GNU Radio 3.10 (fs = 48 kS/s, fc = 10 kHz, μ = 0.75, α = 0.05). The recovered message at block 11 was compared with the source at block 1 after removing the 3.9 ms filter delay.

Noise amplitudeRecovered / source amplitudeOutput SNR
0.5 mV1.1330.1 dB
2 mV (default)1.1324.8 dB
10 mV1.1212.0 dB

Build and run it

  1. Copy the flowgraph text below into a file named m1_waveform_every_block.grc, or build it from the block table and connection list.
  2. Open it in GNU Radio Companion, press F5 then F6. Use headphones; no SDR hardware is needed.
  3. Watch each scope in order 1 → 12, and compare it with the animated diagram above.
  4. Try: raise the noise to 20 mV and listen; set μ above 1 and look at scopes 9 and 12; lower α to 0.01 and see the received signal shrink below the noise.
All 41 blocks: parameters to enter and why each block is used
#Block (Ctrl+F)Why this blockLibraryIDParameters
1Variable48 kS/s: the standard sound-card rate, so the Audio Sink can play the output, and high enough for a 16 kHz carrier.Variablessamp_rateValue 48000
2QT GUI RangeSlider for the carrier frequency. Kept inside the 48 kS/s band so everything stays audible and simulable without radio hardware.GUI Widgets ▸ QTfcLabel "Carrier frequency fc (Hz)" · Default Value 10000 · Start 6000 · Stop 16000 · Step 500
3QT GUI RangeSlider for the modulation index μ. Set it above 1 to see over-modulation in scope 4 and hear the distortion at block 12.GUI Widgets ▸ QTmuLabel "Modulation index mu" · Default Value 0.75 · Start 0.1 · Stop 1.5 · Step 0.05
4QT GUI RangeSlider for channel attenuation α. Shows how a weak received signal is overwhelmed by noise.GUI Widgets ▸ QTalphaLabel "Channel attenuation alpha" · Default Value 0.05 · Start 0.005 · Stop 1 · Step 0.005
5QT GUI RangeSlider for the channel noise amplitude. Raise it and listen to the output become noisy.GUI Widgets ▸ QTnoise_ampLabel "Noise amplitude (V)" · Default Value 0.002 · Stop 0.05 · Step 0.001
6QT GUI RangeLoudspeaker volume, so you can listen comfortably.GUI Widgets ▸ QTvolumeLabel "Loudspeaker volume" · Default Value 0.3 · Stop 1 · Step 0.05
7Signal SourceFirst tone of the “speech-like” information source (500 Hz). Real speech energy is mostly below 1 kHz.Waveform Generatorstone_500Output Type float · Waveform analog.GR_SIN_WAVE · Frequency 500 · Amplitude 0.62
8Signal SourceSecond tone at 1200 Hz with a phase offset, so the source is not a single sine: it behaves more like a voice.Waveform Generatorstone_1200Output Type float · Waveform analog.GR_SIN_WAVE · Frequency 1200 · Amplitude 0.33 · Initial Phase (Radians) 1
9AddAdds the two tones: the sound p(t) produced by the information source (block 1).Math Operatorssrc_soundIO Type float
10ThrottleKeeps the scopes running at real-time speed before the audio card sets the pace. Without it the GUI can freeze in some setups.Miscblocks_throttle2_0Type float
11Multiply ConstMultiply by 0.003: a microphone turns sound pressure into a few millivolts. This models the input transducer (block 2).Math OperatorsmicIO Type float · Constant 0.003
12Multiply ConstMultiply by about 333: the audio amplifier raises the millivolt signal to about 1 V, the level a modulator needs (block 3).Math Operatorsaudio_ampIO Type float · Constant 300/0.9
13Multiply ConstMultiplies the message by μ: sets how strongly the message controls the carrier amplitude.Math Operatorsmod_indexIO Type float · Constant mu
14Add ConstAdds 1 to form 1 + μm(t), so the carrier is transmitted and the envelope stays positive for an envelope detector.Math Operatorsmod_plus_oneIO Type float · Constant 1
15Signal SourceCarrier oscillator at fc: the high-frequency wave that will carry the message.Waveform GeneratorscarrierOutput Type float · Frequency fc
16MultiplyMultiplies 1 + μm(t) by the carrier: the AM wave Ac[1 + μm(t)] cos ωct (block 4).Math Operatorsam_modulatorIO Type float
17Multiply ConstGain of 1 standing for the RF power amplifier and transmitting antenna (block 5). It is a placeholder so the diagram has a scope at the antenna.Math Operatorstx_antennaIO Type float
18Multiply ConstMultiply by α: free-space and other losses make the received signal much weaker (part of block 6).Math Operatorspath_lossIO Type float · Constant alpha
19Noise SourceGaussian noise added in the channel (block 7): the thermal noise every receiver faces.Waveform GeneratorsnoiseOutput Type float · Amplitude noise_amp · Seed 5
20AddAdds attenuated signal and noise: what reaches the receiving antenna.Math OperatorschannelIO Type float
21Band Pass FilterBand-pass filter around fc: the tuned antenna and RF stage select the wanted station and reject noise outside the channel (block 8).Filtersrx_antenna_rfFIR Type fir_filter_fff · Low Cutoff Freq fc - 3500 · High Cutoff Freq fc + 3500 · Transition Width 1000
22AbsAbsolute value = the diode in an envelope detector: it rectifies the AM wave (first half of block 9).Math OperatorsdiodeIO Type float
23Single Pole IIR FilterSingle-pole IIR filter = the RC circuit after the diode. It smooths the rectified wave into the envelope (second half of block 9).FiltersdemodulatorType float · Alpha 0.35
24Low Pass FilterLow-pass filter at 3.4 kHz removes the remaining carrier ripple and noise above the voice band (block 10).Filtersaudio_lpfFIR Type fir_filter_fff · Cutoff Freq 3400 · Transition Width 600
25DC BlockerDC Blocker removes the DC level left by the carrier (block 10), like a coupling capacitor in a radio.FiltersdetectorType ff · Length 256
26Multiply ConstGain that restores the message to its original size: the audio power amplifier (block 11).Math Operatorspower_ampIO Type float · Constant 1/(0.55*alpha*mu)
27Multiply ConstVolume control before the speaker.Math Operatorsloudspeaker_volumeIO Type float · Constant volume
28Audio SinkAudio Sink plays the recovered message through your computer’s sound card: the output transducer and destination (block 12). It also sets the real-time pace of the flowgraph.AudioloudspeakerSample Rate 48000

Block in the live diagramWhat to look atGo to

After the lectures: real hardware in and , programs in , assessment in .

Lecture 1 · M1 Analog Modulation · CO1

Why can't we just shout the song into the sky?

Your voice lives between 300 Hz and 3.4 kHz. To radiate it directly you would need an antenna 25 kilometres long, and every station in the city would collide in the same band. Modulation fixes both problems with one multiplication.

Explain three reasons for modulationProve frequency translation with a trig identitySize an antenna from λ/4Plan an FDM band with guard bands
⏱ 50 minBTL-2 Understand · BTL-3 Apply

ConceptWhat modulation actually does

Modulation is the process of varying one property of a high-frequency carrier \(c(t)=A_c\cos(2\pi f_c t+\phi)\) in step with the message \(m(t)\). A cosine has exactly three knobs, so there are three analog families:

Amplitude → AM

\(A_c\) follows \(m(t)\). Simple receivers, wasteful power.

Frequency → FM

\(f\) swings around \(f_c\) by \(k_f m(t)\). Better noise immunity, more bandwidth.

Phase → PM

\(\phi\) follows \(k_p m(t)\). FM's twin; the basis of PSK and QAM later.

The three reasons we modulate

1 · Practical antennas

An antenna radiates efficiently when its length is comparable to the wavelength, typically \(\lambda/4\). With \(\lambda=c/f\), low frequencies need absurd antennas.

2 · Sharing the spectrum

Every voice signal sits in the same 0–4 kHz band. Put each on a different carrier and they line up side by side: frequency-division multiplexing (FDM).

3 · Matching the channel

Each medium passes some frequencies well (ionosphere, line of sight, cable, fibre). The carrier places the signal where the channel and the hardware work best, and lets us trade bandwidth for noise immunity (FM).

Analogy: the courier vanYour letter (message) cannot fly to Delhi by itself. You put it in a van (carrier) that already knows how to travel the highway (channel). Each company paints its van a different colour (carrier frequency) so the vans share the road without mixing up their letters. At the destination you open the van and take the letter out (demodulation).

BasicsModulation, demodulation and the words around them

Message (modulating) signal

The information \(m(t)\): voice, music or data. Low frequency (baseband).

Carrier

A high-frequency sinusoid \(A_c\cos(2\pi f_ct+\phi)\). It carries no information by itself; it is the vehicle.

Modulated signal

The carrier after one of its knobs has been changed by \(m(t)\). This is what leaves the antenna.

  • Modulation: putting \(m(t)\) onto the carrier, at the transmitter. The frequency is translated up.
  • Demodulation (detection): recovering \(m(t)\) at the receiver. The frequency is translated back down.
  • Modem: modulator + demodulator in one box, for example the DSL or cable modem in a broadband router.
Formal definition. Modulation is changing a parameter (amplitude, frequency or phase) of a carrier in step with the instantaneous value of the message.

BasicsThe family tree of modulation

M1 covers the blue branch. Pulse and digital schemes come in Modules 2 and 3.

AM

Amplitude follows \(m(t)\); frequency and phase fixed.

FM

Frequency follows \(m(t)\); amplitude constant.

PM

Phase follows \(m(t)\). With two levels the phase jumps 0°/180°: BPSK.

PCM (preview)

Sample, quantise and code an analog signal into bits (Module 2).

QAM (preview)

Two carriers 90° apart, each amplitude-modulated: several bits per symbol (Wi-Fi, LTE, 5G).

Polarisation (preview)

Optical links: the angle of the light’s field carries the data.

BasicsAnalog vs digital modulation: same carrier, different message

Analog message → AM

The message takes any value, so the amplitude varies smoothly. FM and PM do the same with the other knobs.

Digital message (bits 1 0 1 1 0) → keying

The carrier is an analog sine wave in both casesOnly the message differs: continuous (analog) or discrete levels (digital). Morse-code telegraphy was the first on-off keying; a broadband modem does modern keying with QPSK and QAM.

BasicsWhat modulation buys, and what it costs

Advantages

  • Practical antenna size (λ/4 is set by the carrier, not the message)
  • Many signals share one medium without mixing (FDM, channels)
  • Wireless links replace long wires over large distances
  • Choose a frequency the channel passes well (ground wave, line of sight, fibre)
  • Trade bandwidth for quality (FM) or quality for simplicity (AM)
  • Narrow relative bandwidth makes filters and amplifiers easy

Costs

  • More complex, costlier transmitter and receiver (oscillators, mixers, filters)
  • Some schemes waste power (AM: ≥ 67 % in the carrier)
  • Some schemes need more bandwidth (wideband FM: 180–200 kHz per station)
  • Coherent receivers need an accurate carrier copy (frequency and phase)
One more term: duty cycleThe fraction of time a transmitter is actually radiating. A phone sends in bursts, so its average RF exposure is lower than its peak power suggests.
ModulationDemodulation
WhereTransmitterReceiver
What it doesPuts the message onto a carrierRecovers the message from the carrier
FrequencyTranslates up: baseband → carrierTranslates down: carrier → baseband
CircuitModulator (mixer, VCO, …)Demodulator (envelope detector, discriminator, PLL, …)
Analog exampleVoice → AM at 1 MHzDiode detector → voice
Digital example (modem)Bits → modulated analog waveformWaveform → bits

AnimatedThe communication system, block by block

Press Play and follow the glowing signal from the information source to the destination. At each block the card explains what the block does, and the scope shows the signal as it leaves that block. Use Next and Back to go at your own pace. Three views go from the simplest model to a full digital system.

DerivationMultiplying by a cosine moves the spectrum

This one result is the engine behind every modulator and demodulator in this module.

  1. Start with a message \(m(t)\) whose Fourier transform \(M(f)\) is zero outside \(|f|\le W\). Multiply by the carrier:

    \[ s(t)=m(t)\cos(2\pi f_c t) \]

  2. Write the cosine with Euler's formula:

    \[ \cos(2\pi f_c t)=\tfrac12\left(e^{j2\pi f_c t}+e^{-j2\pi f_c t}\right) \]

    Why: exponentials are easy to Fourier-transform; cosines are not.

  3. So

    \[ s(t)=\tfrac12\,m(t)e^{j2\pi f_c t}+\tfrac12\,m(t)e^{-j2\pi f_c t} \]

  4. Use the frequency-shift property \(x(t)e^{j2\pi f_0 t}\;\leftrightarrow\;X(f-f_0)\):

    \[ S(f)=\tfrac12 M(f-f_c)+\tfrac12 M(f+f_c) \]

    Simplification: nothing about the shape of \(M(f)\) changes; it is copied, halved, and centred at \(\pm f_c\).

  5. Read the result. The message, which occupied \(-W\dots W\), now occupies \(f_c-W\dots f_c+W\). The part above \(f_c\) is the upper sideband, the part below is the lower sideband, and the bandwidth doubles to

    \[ B_T = 2W \]

  6. Bring it back down. Multiply again by \(\cos(2\pi f_c t)\):

    \[ s(t)\cos(2\pi f_c t)=m(t)\cos^2(2\pi f_c t)=\tfrac12 m(t)+\tfrac12 m(t)\cos(4\pi f_c t) \]

    Why it works: \(\cos^2\theta=\tfrac12(1+\cos2\theta)\). A low-pass filter removes the \(2f_c\) term and leaves \(\tfrac12 m(t)\): that is coherent demodulation, Lecture 3.

\[ m(t)\cos(2\pi f_c t)\;\longleftrightarrow\;\tfrac12\left[M(f-f_c)+M(f+f_c)\right] \]The modulation theorem: multiplication in time = shift in frequency

Antenna length from the wavelength

  1. \[ \lambda=\frac{c}{f},\qquad c=3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s} \]
  2. \[ L_{\lambda/4}=\frac{c}{4f} \]

    Rule of thumb: \(L\,[\text{m}]\approx 75/f\,[\text{MHz}]\). At 100 MHz that is 0.75 m: the length of an FM whip.

InteractiveHow long must the antenna be?

Drag from 1 kHz (raw audio) to 3 GHz (Wi-Fi). Compare the quarter-wave antenna with a person, a tower and a mobile phone.

Frequency-division multiplexing at a glance

Three 4 kHz voices on DSB carriers 9 kHz apart: each needs 8 kHz, leaving a 1 kHz guard band. That is exactly how Indian medium-wave stations are spaced (9 kHz).

Worked examplesNumbers you can check with a calculator

Example 1 · Antenna for raw speech λ/4
Given: speech at \(f=3\) kHz. Find: a quarter-wave antenna, then the same after modulating onto 1 MHz and 100 MHz.

\(\lambda=\dfrac{3\times10^8}{3\times10^3}=10^5\ \text{m}=100\ \text{km}\Rightarrow L=\lambda/4=25\ \text{km}\).

At 1 MHz: \(\lambda=300\) m, \(L=75\) m (a medium-wave mast). At 100 MHz: \(\lambda=3\) m, \(L=0.75\) m.

Answer: 25 km → 75 m → 0.75 m. Modulation shrinks the antenna by a factor of \(f_c/f_m\).

Example 2 · Your favourite FM station λ/4
Given: \(f_c=98.3\) MHz. Find: the quarter-wave whip length.

\(\lambda=3\times10^8/98.3\times10^6=3.052\) m, so \(L=0.763\) m. Phone earphone cables (≈ 1 m) act as the FM antenna for exactly this reason.

Answer: L ≈ 76 cm.

Example 3 · Planning an FDM group multiplexing
Given: 5 voice channels, each 4 kHz wide, with 1 kHz guard bands between neighbours. Find: total bandwidth with SSB and with DSB.

SSB: each channel needs \(W=4\) kHz → \(5\times4+4\times1=24\) kHz.

DSB: each needs \(2W=8\) kHz → \(5\times8+4\times1=44\) kHz.

Answer: 24 kHz (SSB), 44 kHz (DSB). Halving the bandwidth is why telephone FDM used SSB.

Example 4 · Fractional bandwidth hardware view
Given: hi-fi audio 20 Hz – 20 kHz. Find: the ratio of highest to lowest frequency before and after DSB modulation onto 1 MHz.

Baseband: \(20\,000/20=1000\) (a 3-decade span; no single antenna or amplifier is flat over that).

Modulated: band 0.98 – 1.02 MHz, ratio \(1.02/0.98=1.04\): only 4 %.

Answer: 1000 : 1 → 1.04 : 1. A narrow relative band makes filters, amplifiers and antennas easy to design.

PracticeYour turn: type the answer and check

Level 1

Quarter-wave antenna length at 1 MHz, in metres?

Level 1

Quarter-wave length at 2.4 GHz (Wi-Fi), in centimetres?

Level 2

A 1 MHz carrier is DSB-modulated by a 2 kHz tone. The upper sideband is at 1002 kHz. Where is the lower sideband, in kHz?

Level 3

How many 8 kHz DSB channels with 1 kHz guards fit in a 98 kHz band? (n channels need 8n + (n−1) kHz.)

Real worldWhere you meet modulation today

Medium-wave AM

531–1602 kHz in India. Masts are 50–150 m tall because λ/4 at 1 MHz is 75 m.

FM radio

88–108 MHz. The whip on a car or the headphone cable in your phone is the antenna.

Your phone

LTE/5G bands 700 MHz – 3.6 GHz: antennas are a few centimetres, printed inside the case.

Real worldWhere each scheme is used

SchemeUsed inCovered in
AM (DSB-FC)Medium-wave broadcast (AIR), aviation VHF voiceM1 · L2, L3, L7
SSBHF ham radio, marine and military HF voiceM1 · L9
FMFM broadcast, analog TV sound, two-way radios, walkie-talkiesM1 · L4, L5, L8
PMArmstrong FM transmitters, deep-space telemetryM1 · L6
ASK / OOKOptical fibre with LEDs (light on = 1), 433 MHz remote keys, RFIDM2
FSK / GFSKBluetooth, old dial-up modems, pagers, many IoT sensorsM2
PSK / QAMWi-Fi, LTE, 5G, satellite TV, cable modems (QPSK to 1024-QAM)M2, M4
Pulse (PWM, PCM)Motor and LED dimming, class-D audio (PWM); 64 kb/s telephone voice (PCM)M2, M3

Common mistakesAvoid these in the exam

  • Saying modulation "amplifies" the signal. It translates it in frequency; power is a separate matter.
  • Forgetting that DSB doubles the bandwidth: \(B_T=2W\), not \(W\).
  • Using \(\lambda=f/c\). It is \(\lambda=c/f\): higher frequency, shorter wave.

Read criticallyStatements you will find online, corrected

Popular tutorial sites repeat these. Check every claim against first principles.

ClaimCorrection
✗ “Modulation increases the strength of the signal.”✓ Modulation translates the signal in frequency. Strength comes from the power amplifier and the antenna.
✗ “The antenna must be 1/10 of the wavelength.”✓ Efficient antennas are typically λ/4 (monopole) or λ/2 (dipole). Much shorter ones work, but poorly.
✗ “Modulation converts digital to analog.”✓ Only in a modem. AM, FM and PM map an analog message to an analog signal.
✗ “A 100 MHz FM antenna is 80 cm.”✓ λ = 3 m, so λ/4 = 75 cm (≈ 71 cm after the usual 5 % shortening).
✗ “A high-frequency carrier travels without being affected by noise or interference.”✓ Noise adds to any signal at any frequency. High frequency helps with antennas and channel choice; FM’s noise advantage comes from its bandwidth (L5).
✗ “Baseband signals must be modulated to increase their strength.”✓ Strength comes from amplifiers. Baseband is at the wrong frequency for antennas and sharing; wired links like USB send baseband directly.
✗ “ASK has high bandwidth efficiency, FSK higher SNR, PSK susceptibility to errors.”✓ Binary ASK and PSK need the same bandwidth; FSK needs more. For the same Eb/N0, BPSK has the lowest error rate (Module 2).

Explore, answeredThree investigations worked through

1 · Count the FM stations with SDR++

Connect an RTL-SDR or HackRF as shown in , open SDR++, choose the source, set the centre to 98 MHz and the sample rate to 2.4 MS/s (RTL-SDR) or 20 MS/s (HackRF, which shows the whole 88–108 MHz band at once). Step through the band, note every peak, and subtract neighbours. L8 has a simulated band to practise on and a worksheet.

How to connect: SDR → laptop → SDR++

  1. Antenna to SDR. Screw the dipole (RTL-SDR) or the telescopic antenna (HackRF, ANT port) onto the SMA socket. Pull each arm out to about 75 cm, the λ/4 for 100 MHz.

  2. SDR to laptop. Plug into a USB 2.0/3.0 port, through a short extension cable so the dongle sits away from laptop noise. Check with rtl_test or hackrf_info.

  3. Open SDR++. Source panel → RTL-SDR (sample rate 2.4 MS/s, gain about 30 dB) or HackRF (20 MS/s, LNA 16–24 dB, VGA 20–30 dB, amp off). Press ▶.

  4. Tune and demodulate. Centre 98 MHz, Radio → WFM, bandwidth 200 kHz. Click each peak in the waterfall, note its frequency, and subtract neighbours to get the spacing.

Expect

Peaks about 180–200 kHz wide: Carson gives 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz.

Spacing

Neighbouring stations sit a whole number of channel steps apart; stations in one city are usually spaced several hundred kHz or more apart so receivers do not overlap.

Look closer

Zoom on one station: the 19 kHz stereo pilot and the 38 kHz L−R band from Lecture 7 are visible after WFM demodulation.

2 · Wavelength-division multiplexing: FDM at 193 THz

An optical fibre carries many lasers at once, each at a different wavelength. That is FDM: separate carriers, guard bands, and a filter at the receiver picks one. Only the numbers change.

How it is connected: a DWDM fibre link

The carrier

\[f=\frac{c}{\lambda}=\frac{3\times10^8}{1550\times10^{-9}}\approx193.4\ \text{THz}\]

The ITU-T G.694.1 grid is anchored at 193.1 THz, with channels at 100 GHz (0.8 nm) or 50 GHz (0.4 nm) spacing in the C-band (≈ 1530–1565 nm).

How many channels?

The C-band is about 4.4 THz wide: \(4.4\text{ THz}/100\text{ GHz}\approx44\) channels, or about 88 at 50 GHz. Commercial systems quote 40 and 80 channels.

FM radio (FDM)DWDM fibre
Carrier88–108 MHz≈ 192–196 THz
Channel spacing200 kHz raster100 or 50 GHz
Channel filterIF filter in a superhetoptical demultiplexer (thin-film or arrayed waveguide)
Fractional spacing200 k / 100 M = 0.2 %100 G / 193 T ≈ 0.05 %

3 · Why submarine antennas are kilometres long

Seawater is a good conductor (σ ≈ 4 S/m), so radio waves die out within a few skin depths:

\[ \delta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f\mu_0\sigma}} \]

At 100 MHz (FM)

\(\delta\approx2.5\) cm. FM cannot reach a submerged submarine.

At 18.2 kHz (VLF)

\(\delta\approx1.9\) m. Each skin depth costs 8.7 dB, so 20 m depth costs ≈ 93 dB: hard, but a sensitive receiver and a megawatt transmitter make it work. VLF reaches roughly 10–40 m.

The antenna

VLF is 3–30 kHz, so λ = 100–10 km and λ/4 at 30 kHz is 2.5 km. Real stations use huge umbrella or top-loaded arrays that are still electrically short, radiating only 10–50 % of the transmitter power.

How it is connected: a VLF shore-to-submarine link

India's VLF stationINS Kattabomman at Vijayanarayanam, Tamil Nadu (commissioned 1990) transmits on VLF around 16–19 kHz from a field of 13 masts in two rings around a 301 m central mast, about 3,000 acres. The bandwidth of such an antenna is only tens of hertz, so data rates are a few hundred bit/s at most (MSK up to about 300 bit/s): enough for short text messages, which is all a submarine needs.

Sources: Wikipedia, “Very low frequency” and “INS Kattabomman”; ITU-T G.694.1 DWDM grid (via ProLabs grid table). Skin-depth numbers computed with σ = 4 S/m.

Lecture 2 · M1 Analog Modulation · CO1

Amplitude modulation: the envelope carries the song

A 10 kW AM transmitter playing a tone at the safest setting spends only 1.1 kW on the information. Where does the rest go, and why do broadcasters still do it?

Derive the AM spectrumFind μ from a scope traceCompute carrier, sideband and total powerExplain over-modulation
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply · BTL-4 Analyse

ConceptThe canonical AM signal

Add a constant to the message so it never goes negative, then let it set the carrier's amplitude:

\[ s(t)=\big[A_c+m(t)\big]\cos(\omega_c t),\qquad \omega_c=2\pi f_c \]

The bracket \(A_c+m(t)\) is the envelope. As long as it stays positive, the outline of the waveform is an exact copy of the message shifted up by \(A_c\). That is what lets a single diode recover the audio (Lecture 3).

Normalise the message by its peak and define the modulation index:

\[ s(t)=A_c\big[1+\mu\,m_n(t)\big]\cos(\omega_c t),\qquad \mu=\frac{\max|m(t)|}{A_c},\quad |m_n(t)|\le1 \]

μ < 1

Under-modulated. Envelope never touches zero. Safe, but weak sidebands.

μ = 1

100 % modulation. Envelope just touches zero. Maximum efficiency for envelope detection.

μ > 1

Over-modulation. Envelope crosses zero and the carrier phase flips: distortion and splatter into neighbouring channels.

Analogy: the volume knobImagine a lamp flickering 1 million times per second (too fast to see). Your message turns its brightness knob up and down slowly. Someone far away cannot see the flicker, only the slow brightness changes: that is the envelope, and that is your message.

DerivationBuilding AM step by step: from m(t) and c(t) to s(t)

An AM transmitter needs only two operations: an adder that lifts the message above zero, and a product modulator (a multiplier) that puts it on the carrier.

  1. Start with a single-tone message and a high-frequency carrier:

    \[m(t)=A_m\cos(2\pi f_mt),\qquad c(t)=A_c\cos(2\pi f_ct),\qquad f_c\gg f_m\]

  2. Adder: add the DC level \(A_c\) and take it out as a common factor:

    \[v(t)=A_c+A_m\cos\omega_mt=A_c\left[1+\mu\cos\omega_mt\right],\qquad \mu=\frac{A_m}{A_c}\]

    Why: with \(A_m<A_c\) (μ < 1), \(v(t)\) never goes negative, so the envelope of the final signal is an exact copy of the message.

  3. Product modulator: multiply \(v(t)\) by the carrier:

    \[s(t)=v(t)\cdot\cos\omega_ct=\left[A_c+A_m\cos\omega_mt\right]\cos\omega_ct\]

  4. Multiply out the bracket:

    \[s(t)=A_c\cos\omega_ct+A_m\cos\omega_mt\,\cos\omega_ct\]

  5. Product-to-sum on the second term, with \(A_m=\mu A_c\):

    \[\cos A\cos B=\tfrac12\left[\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)\right]\]
    \[s(t)=\underbrace{A_c\cos\omega_ct}_{\text{carrier}}+\underbrace{\frac{\mu A_c}{2}\cos(\omega_c+\omega_m)t}_{\text{upper sideband}}+\underbrace{\frac{\mu A_c}{2}\cos(\omega_c-\omega_m)t}_{\text{lower sideband}}\]

  6. Frequency domain: the message line at \(f_m\) is translated to both sides of the carrier.

    For any message band-limited to \(W\):

    \[S(f)=\frac{A_c}{2}\left[\delta(f-f_c)+\delta(f+f_c)\right]+\frac12\left[M(f-f_c)+M(f+f_c)\right]\] \[B_T=(f_c+f_m)-(f_c-f_m)=2f_m\qquad(\text{in general } B_T=2W)\]
Textbook formMany books write \(s(t)=A_c\left[1+k_a\,m(t)\right]\cos\omega_ct\), where \(k_a\) is the amplitude sensitivity (per volt). It is the same signal, with \(\mu=k_aA_m\).
Numerical check plug in numbers
Given: \(A_c=10\) V, \(A_m=5\) V, \(f_c=100\) kHz, \(f_m=5\) kHz.

\(\mu=5/10=0.5\); each sideband \(\mu A_c/2=2.5\) V.

\[s(t)=10\cos(2\pi\cdot100\text{k}\,t)+2.5\cos(2\pi\cdot105\text{k}\,t)+2.5\cos(2\pi\cdot95\text{k}\,t)\]

Lines: 10 V at 100 kHz; 2.5 V at 95 and 105 kHz. Bandwidth 10 kHz.

Why the DC matters: without \(A_c\), the product \(m(t)\cos\omega_ct\) is DSB-SC; its envelope is \(|m(t)|\) and an envelope detector fails (Lecture 9).

ConceptThe AM family: four members, one idea

DSB-FC (standard AM)

Carrier + both sidebands
Bandwidth: 2W
Power in sidebands: ≤ 33 %
Used in: MW broadcast, aviation

DSB-SC

Both sidebands, no carrier
Bandwidth: 2W
Power in sidebands: 100 %
Used in: FM stereo L−R, the building block of QAM

SSB

Bandwidth: W
Power in sidebands: 100 %

VSB

One sideband + a vestige of the other
Bandwidth: ≈ 1.25W
Power in sidebands: carrier kept in TV
Used in: Analog TV video

This lecture is standard AM (DSB-FC). DSB-SC, SSB and VSB, the carrier-saving members, are in

ContextA little history, and the labels on real radios

History

In the early 1900s Reginald Fessenden (Canada/USA) and Roberto Landell de Moura (Brazil) experimented with sending voice by radiotelephone. AM became the first voice broadcasting method because a crystal or diode receiver can demodulate it with almost no parts.

Medium-wave AM broadcasting spread worldwide from the 1920s. In India the Indian State Broadcasting Service (1930) was renamed All India Radio in 1936.

ITU emission codes

A3EDouble-sideband, full carrier: standard AM broadcast
H3ESingle sideband, full carrier
R3ESingle sideband, reduced carrier
J3ESingle sideband, suppressed carrier: HF voice
B8EIndependent sidebands (two different signals)
C3FVestigial sideband: analog TV video

Read the code: 1st letter = type of modulation, 3 = one analog channel, E = telephony (voice), F = television.

DerivationSingle-tone AM: spectrum and power

  1. Take a tone \(m(t)=A_m\cos\omega_m t\), so \(\mu=A_m/A_c\):

    \[ s(t)=A_c\cos\omega_c t+\mu A_c\cos\omega_m t\cos\omega_c t \]

  2. Product-to-sum identity:

    \[\cos A\cos B=\tfrac12[\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)]\]\[ s(t)=\underbrace{A_c\cos\omega_c t}_{\text{carrier}}+\underbrace{\tfrac{\mu A_c}{2}\cos(\omega_c+\omega_m)t}_{\text{USB}}+\underbrace{\tfrac{\mu A_c}{2}\cos(\omega_c-\omega_m)t}_{\text{LSB}} \]

    Read it: three spectral lines at \(f_c\), \(f_c\pm f_m\). Bandwidth \(B_T=2f_m\) (for a general message, \(2W\)).

  3. Power of a sinusoid of amplitude \(A\) in a resistor \(R\) is \(A^2/2R\). So

    \[ P_c=\frac{A_c^2}{2R},\qquad P_{USB}=P_{LSB}=\frac{(\mu A_c/2)^2}{2R}=\frac{\mu^2}{4}P_c \]

  4. Add them:

    \[ P_t=P_c\left(1+\frac{\mu^2}{2}\right) \]

    Simplification: the three lines are at different frequencies, so they are orthogonal and their powers simply add.

  5. Efficiency = useful (sideband) power ÷ total power:

    \[ \eta=\frac{P_{USB}+P_{LSB}}{P_t}=\frac{\mu^2/2}{1+\mu^2/2}=\frac{\mu^2}{2+\mu^2} \]

    Best case \(\mu=1\): \(\eta=1/3\). At least two-thirds of the power is spent on the carrier, which carries no information.

  6. Antenna current. Since \(P\propto I^2\):

    \[ I_t=I_c\sqrt{1+\mu^2/2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \mu=\sqrt{2\left[(I_t/I_c)^2-1\right]} \]

  7. μ from the oscilloscope. The envelope swings between \(A_{max}=A_c(1+\mu)\) and \(A_{min}=A_c(1-\mu)\). Subtract and add:

    \[ \mu=\frac{A_{max}-A_{min}}{A_{max}+A_{min}},\qquad A_c=\frac{A_{max}+A_{min}}{2} \]

  8. Several tones with indices \(\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots\): their sideband powers add, so

    \[ \mu_t=\sqrt{\mu_1^2+\mu_2^2+\cdots},\qquad P_t=P_c\left(1+\frac{\mu_t^2}{2}\right) \]
\[ s(t)=A_c\cos\omega_ct+\tfrac{\mu A_c}{2}\cos(\omega_c\pm\omega_m)t,\quad P_t=P_c\Big(1+\tfrac{\mu^2}{2}\Big),\quad \eta=\tfrac{\mu^2}{2+\mu^2} \]Everything about tone AM in one line

NoteSame AM, other textbooks: the sine form and a subtle point

NCERT and many textbooks write the carrier and message with sines: \(c(t)=A_c\sin\omega_ct\), \(m(t)=A_m\sin\omega_mt\). Then

\[s(t)=(A_c+A_m\sin\omega_mt)\sin\omega_ct=A_c\sin\omega_ct+\frac{\mu A_c}{2}\cos(\omega_c-\omega_m)t-\frac{\mu A_c}{2}\cos(\omega_c+\omega_m)t\]

Same three lines, same bandwidth \(2f_m\), same \(\mu=A_m/A_c\). Only the phase reference differs.

Subtle point: the carrier line does not changeIn the spectrum the carrier component keeps the same amplitude \(A_c\) whatever the message does. The envelope moves because the two sidebands add to and subtract from it. Switch the modulation off and only the sidebands disappear.

Advantages of AM

  • Simple to generate and to demodulate (one diode)
  • Cheapest receivers of any scheme
  • Long reach on medium and short wave

Disadvantages of AM

  • Power-hungry: ≥ 67 % of the power in the carrier
  • Needs \(2W\) of bandwidth: twice the audio bandwidth (not equal to it, as some sources say)
  • Amplitude noise and interference go straight into the audio

Worked examplesExam-style problems, fully solved

Example 1 · Complete tone-AM analysis spectrum + power
Given: \(A_c=10\) V, \(A_m=5\) V, \(f_c=1\) MHz, \(f_m=5\) kHz, load \(R=50\ \Omega\).

\(\mu=5/10=0.5\). Lines: 1 MHz at 10 V; 1.005 MHz and 0.995 MHz at \(\mu A_c/2=2.5\) V each. \(B_T=2f_m=10\) kHz.

\(P_c=10^2/(2\cdot50)=1\) W; each sideband \(\mu^2P_c/4=0.0625\) W; \(P_t=1(1+0.125)=1.125\) W; \(\eta=0.25/2.25=11.1\%\).

Answer: B = 10 kHz, P_t = 1.125 W, only 0.125 W carries the tone.

Example 2 · Reading μ from a trace envelope
Given: envelope peaks at 14 V, troughs at 6 V.

\(\mu=(14-6)/(14+6)=0.4\); \(A_c=(14+6)/2=10\) V; \(A_m=\mu A_c=4\) V.

Answer: μ = 0.4 (40 % modulation).

Example 3 · From power meter to μ transmitter
Given: unmodulated carrier 10 kW; modulated total 11.8 kW.

\(1+\mu^2/2=11.8/10=1.18\Rightarrow\mu^2=0.36\Rightarrow\mu=0.6\).

Answer: μ = 0.6, sideband power 1.8 kW.

Example 4 · From antenna ammeter to μ current
Given: antenna current 8 A unmodulated, 8.93 A modulated.

\((8.93/8)^2=1.246=1+\mu^2/2\Rightarrow\mu^2=0.492\Rightarrow\mu=0.70\).

Answer: μ ≈ 0.70.

Example 5 · Two tones at once multi-tone
Given: \(P_c=1\) kW, tones with \(\mu_1=0.3\), \(\mu_2=0.4\).

\(\mu_t=\sqrt{0.09+0.16}=0.5\); \(P_t=1(1+0.25/2)=1.125\) kW. Bandwidth is set by the higher tone.

Answer: μ_t = 0.5, P_t = 1.125 kW.

Example 6 · A textbook classic sine form
Given: carrier 1 MHz, peak 20 V; message 1 kHz, peak 10 V. Find μ, the frequencies present and the bandwidth.

\(\mu=A_m/A_c=10/20=0.5\) (50 % modulation).

Frequencies: \(f_c=1000\) kHz, \(f_c+f_m=1001\) kHz (USB), \(f_c-f_m=999\) kHz (LSB). Bandwidth \(=1001-999=2\) kHz \(=2f_m\).

Answer: μ = 0.5; lines at 999, 1000, 1001 kHz; B = 2 kHz.

Example 7 · Recognise AM from a sum of cosines exam favourite
Given: \(y(t)=10\cos(1800\pi t)+20\cos(2000\pi t)+10\cos(2200\pi t)\). Find \(f_c\), \(f_m\), μ and the bandwidth.

The middle, largest term is the carrier: \(\omega_c=2000\pi\Rightarrow f_c=1000\) Hz, \(A_c=20\).

The outer terms at 900 and 1100 Hz are the sidebands \(f_c\pm f_m\Rightarrow f_m=100\) Hz.

Each sideband \(=\mu A_c/2=10\Rightarrow\mu=2\cdot10/20=1\). Check: \(10[\cos1800\pi t+\cos2200\pi t]=20\cos2000\pi t\cos200\pi t\). Bandwidth \(=2f_m=200\) Hz.

Answer: f_c = 1 kHz, f_m = 100 Hz, μ = 1 (100 %), B = 200 Hz.

Short answersFive questions you will see in exams

Q1 · Why is the carrier frequency much higher than the message frequency?

A small antenna (λ/4), less mixing between stations (FDM), and a narrow relative bandwidth that is easy to filter and amplify.

Q2 · Define the modulation index μ.

\(\mu=A_m/A_c\), the ratio of message amplitude to carrier amplitude (× 100 % for percentage modulation).

Q3 · What happens if μ > 1?

Over-modulation: the envelope crosses zero, the carrier phase reverses, the envelope detector output is distorted and extra sidebands splatter into neighbouring channels.

Q4 · Why keep \(A_m<A_c\)?

To keep μ < 1, so the envelope never reaches zero and a simple envelope detector recovers \(m(t)\) without distortion.

Q5 · AM or FM: which is preferred, and why?

For quality, FM: it trades extra bandwidth for much better noise immunity (L5). For cheap, long-range receivers, or for aviation, AM.

Hardware labBuild AM on a breadboard

One AD633 analog multiplier makes standard AM. It computes \(W=\frac{(X_1-X_2)(Y_1-Y_2)}{10\,\text{V}}+Z\). Feed the carrier to \(X_1\), the message to \(Y_1\), and tie \(Z\) to \(X_1\). The output is then

\[W=V_c\cos\omega_ct\left[1+\frac{V_m}{10\,\text{V}}\cos\omega_mt\right],\qquad \mu=\frac{V_m}{10\,\text{V}}\]

A 1N4148 diode with 10 kΩ ∥ 10 nF (RC = 100 µs) recovers the 1 kHz message. Remove the X1 → Z jumper and the same circuit makes DSB-SC.

Function generator CH2 → Y1 (pin 3)Message: sine, 1 kHz, 10 Vpp, so μ = 0.5

The lab page shows the build in 3D, step by step: every component and wire on its hole, the instruments with their leads, a full wiring table, and a live oscilloscope where you can change μ, the detector capacitor and the Z jumper.

Real worldWhy AM survives

Cheap receivers

A crystal set with no battery can play AM: one diode, one capacitor, one earphone.

Long reach

Medium-wave ground waves follow the Earth's curve for hundreds of kilometres; at night the sky wave goes further.

Aviation

Air-traffic voice (118–137 MHz) is AM: two pilots transmitting together are both heard rather than one silently blocking the other.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Writing the sideband amplitude as \(\mu A_c\). It is \(\mu A_c/2\) for each sideband.
  • Using \(P_t=P_c(1+\mu^2)\). The correct factor is \(1+\mu^2/2\).
  • Adding indices of several tones linearly. They add as a root-sum-square.

Lecture 3 · M1 Analog Modulation · CO1

Getting the message back: a diode, a capacitor, and a lot of noise

The cheapest AM receiver ever built costs less than ₹20. Pick its capacitor wrongly and the voice turns to buzz or gets clipped. Pick the carrier phase wrongly in a coherent receiver and the voice disappears completely.

Design the RC of an envelope detectorDerive the diagonal-clipping limitAnalyse phase and frequency error in coherent detectionCompare AM and DSB noise performance
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply · BTL-4 Analyse

ConceptTwo ways to demodulate AM

Envelope detector (non-coherent)

A diode lets the positive peaks through; a capacitor holds each peak; a resistor lets the capacitor discharge slowly so it can follow the envelope down. Needs no carrier, works only for full-carrier AM with \(\mu\le1\).

Synchronous detector (coherent)

Multiply by a locally generated copy of the carrier and low-pass filter. Works for AM, DSB-SC and SSB, but the local carrier must match the received carrier in frequency and phase.

Analogy: the leaky bucketThe capacitor is a bucket filled by a hose that spurts a million times a second (the carrier peaks). A small leak (the resistor) lets the level fall. If the leak is too slow, the level cannot drop fast enough when the music gets quieter (diagonal clipping). If it is too fast, the level sags between spurts (ripple).

DerivationChoosing RC, and what coherent detection really outputs

A · The envelope detector time constant

  1. Smooth the carrier: between carrier peaks (period \(T_c=1/f_c\)) the capacitor must barely discharge:

    \[ RC\gg T_c=\frac1{f_c} \]

  2. Follow the envelope: the envelope is \(e(t)=A_c(1+\mu\cos\omega_m t)\). During discharge the capacitor voltage falls as \(v\,e^{-t/RC}\), i.e. at rate \(v/RC\). It can follow only if the envelope never falls faster:

    \[ \left|\frac{de}{dt}\right|\le\frac{e(t)}{RC}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\mu\,\omega_m\sin\omega_m t}{1+\mu\cos\omega_m t}\le\frac1{RC} \]

  3. Find the worst instant. Differentiate the left side with respect to \(x=\omega_m t\) and set it to zero:

    \[ \cos x(1+\mu\cos x)+\mu\sin^2x=0\;\Rightarrow\;\cos x=-\mu,\quad \sin x=\sqrt{1-\mu^2} \]

    Simplification: \(\cos^2x+\sin^2x=1\) collapses the expression to \(\cos x+\mu=0\).

  4. Substitute back: the largest value is \(\mu\omega_m/\sqrt{1-\mu^2}\). Therefore

    \[ \frac1{f_c}\ll RC\le\frac{\sqrt{1-\mu^2}}{\mu\,\omega_m} \]

    Check the limits: as \(\mu\to1\) the right side goes to zero. At 100 % modulation no finite RC avoids clipping at the deepest trough, which is why broadcasters keep μ a little below 1.

B · Coherent detection with phase and frequency error

  1. Received DSB-SC \(s(t)=A_c m(t)\cos\omega_c t\); local oscillator \(2\cos[(\omega_c+\Delta\omega)t+\phi]\):

    \[ v(t)=A_c m(t)\left[\cos(\Delta\omega t+\phi)+\cos\big((2\omega_c+\Delta\omega)t+\phi\big)\right] \]

  2. The low-pass filter removes the \(2\omega_c\) term:

    \[ y(t)=A_c\,m(t)\cos(\Delta\omega\,t+\phi) \]

  3. Phase error only (\(\Delta\omega=0\)): \(y=A_c m(t)\cos\phi\). A constant attenuation, zero at \(\phi=90^\circ\): the quadrature null effect.

    Frequency error only (\(\phi=0\)): \(y=A_c m(t)\cos(\Delta\omega t)\). The voice fades in and out at \(\Delta f\): the "warble" heard on a mistuned SSB radio.

    Fix: recover the carrier with a PLL or a Costas loop (Lecture 5), or transmit a pilot carrier.

C · Noise performance in one table

Define the baseband reference \(\gamma=\dfrac{P_r}{N_0W}\): the SNR you would get by sending the message without modulation over the same channel. The figure of merit \(\text{SNR}_o/\gamma\) compares systems fairly.

  1. DSB-SC, coherent: signal and in-phase noise are both shifted down; the quadrature noise is rejected. Result \(\text{SNR}_o=\gamma\), figure of merit 1.

  2. AM, envelope, high SNR: the carrier contributes power but no information, so only the sideband fraction counts:

    \[ \text{SNR}_o=\frac{\mu^2P_{m}}{1+\mu^2P_{m}}\,\gamma\;\xrightarrow{\text{tone},\ \mu=1}\;\frac13\gamma \]

    Cost: AM is at least 4.8 dB worse than DSB-SC. Below a carrier-to-noise ratio of roughly 10 dB the envelope detector also shows a threshold effect: the message is lost in noise.

SystemDetectorFigure of merit SNRₒ/γBandwidth
AM (tone, μ = 1)envelope1/3 (−4.8 dB)2W
DSB-SCcoherent1 (0 dB)2W
SSBcoherent1 (0 dB)W

InteractiveDesign the envelope detector

Carrier 20 kHz, message 500 Hz (scaled down so you can see individual carrier cycles). Try RC = 50 µs (ripple) and 1000 µs (clipping). Grey: AM signal; dashed: ideal envelope; orange: capacitor voltage.

Worked examplesDesign and analysis

Example 1 · Choose R and C envelope detector
Given: \(f_c=1\) MHz, \(f_m=5\) kHz, \(\mu=0.6\).

Lower bound: \(RC\gg1\ \mu\text{s}\). Upper bound: \(\dfrac{\sqrt{1-0.36}}{0.6\cdot2\pi\cdot5000}=\dfrac{0.8}{18\,850}=42.4\ \mu\text{s}\).

Choose \(RC=20\ \mu\)s: for example \(R=10\ \text{k}\Omega\), \(C=2\) nF. It is 20 × the carrier period and half the clipping limit.

Answer: 1 µs ≪ RC ≤ 42.4 µs; RC = 20 µs (10 kΩ, 2 nF).

Example 2 · Largest safe μ clipping
Given: \(RC=50\ \mu\)s, \(f_m=4\) kHz.

\(RC\,\omega_m=50\times10^{-6}\cdot2\pi\cdot4000=1.257\). Need \(\sqrt{1-\mu^2}/\mu\ge1.257\Rightarrow 1/\mu^2\ge1+1.579=2.579\Rightarrow\mu\le0.623\).

Answer: μ ≤ 0.62; above that the 4 kHz tone is diagonally clipped.

Example 3 · Phase error coherent
Given: coherent DSB-SC detector with LO phase error 30°, 60°, 90°.

Output factor \(\cos\phi\): 0.866 (−1.25 dB), 0.5 (−6.02 dB), 0 (silence).

Answer: −1.25 dB, −6.02 dB, total loss at 90°.

Example 4 · Frequency error coherent
Given: LO is 20 Hz off; message is a 1 kHz tone.

\(y(t)=A_c\cos(2\pi1000t)\cos(2\pi20t)\): the tone's loudness swings with a 50 ms period and goes silent every 25 ms.

Answer: a 1 kHz tone "pulsing" 40 times a second.

Example 5 · AM vs DSB-SC noise figure of merit
Given: \(\gamma=30\) dB (1000), tone with \(\mu=0.5\).

AM: \(\text{SNR}_o=\dfrac{\mu^2/2}{1+\mu^2/2}\gamma=\dfrac{0.125}{1.125}\cdot1000=111\Rightarrow20.5\) dB. DSB-SC: 30 dB.

Answer: AM is 9.5 dB worse at μ = 0.5 (4.8 dB worse at best).

Real worldDetectors you can hold

Crystal radio

A germanium diode (OA79/1N34) and the capacitance of a high-impedance earphone: the envelope detector of this lecture.

Superheterodyne AM set

Converts every station to a fixed 455 kHz IF, then uses an envelope detector there.

SSB ham radio

Coherent detection with a "clarifier" knob: you tune the LO by ear until the voice stops sounding like Donald Duck.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Choosing RC "as large as possible" for smoothness. Too large causes diagonal clipping.
  • Using an envelope detector for DSB-SC. Without a carrier the envelope is \(|m(t)|\), not \(m(t)\).
  • Forgetting the factor 2 on the local oscillator. \(\cos^2\) gives ½; the LO amplitude 2 cancels it.

Lecture 4 · M1 Analog Modulation · CO1

Frequency modulation: constant amplitude, swinging frequency

An FM transmitter's output power never changes, whatever the music does. Yet tune β to exactly 2.405 and the carrier line vanishes from the spectrum completely. Bessel functions explain both.

Define instantaneous frequency and phaseDerive the Bessel spectrum of tone FMUse Carson's rule and the 1 % ruleDistinguish narrowband and wideband FM
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply · BTL-4 Analyse

ConceptInstantaneous frequency

For any angle-modulated wave \(s(t)=A_c\cos\theta(t)\), the instantaneous frequency is the rate at which the angle turns:

\[ f_i(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\frac{d\theta(t)}{dt} \]

In FM we make that frequency follow the message:

\[ f_i(t)=f_c+k_f\,m(t)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta(t)=2\pi f_ct+2\pi k_f\!\int_0^t m(\tau)\,d\tau \] \[ s_{FM}(t)=A_c\cos\!\Big[2\pi f_ct+2\pi k_f\!\int_0^t m(\tau)\,d\tau\Big] \]

Frequency sensitivity \(k_f\)

Hz per volt. How far the frequency moves per volt of message.

Peak deviation \(\Delta f\)

\(\Delta f=k_f\max|m(t)|\). Broadcast FM: 75 kHz.

Deviation ratio / index

\(\beta=\Delta f/f_m\) (tone) or \(D=\Delta f/W\). Sets bandwidth and noise immunity.

Analogy: the sirenAn ambulance siren keeps the same loudness but its pitch slides up and down. How far the pitch slides is the deviation Δf; how often it slides is the message frequency f_m. Your ear (a frequency detector) hears the pattern of the slides, which is the message.

Block diagramBuilding FM directly: a bias and a VCO

Press Next to build the system one block at a time, the same order as the lecture slides. Each step lights up a block and the scope trace it produces.

Swipe the diagram sideways to see the whole chain.

Voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO)

Its output frequency follows its input voltage: an LC tank tuned by a varactor diode, or the VCO inside a PLL chip such as the CD4046. The bias sets fc; the message swings it by ±Δf = kf·Am.

Why is the amplitude constant?

Only the frequency moves, so Ac and the power Ac²/2 never change (dashed lines in ③). The receiver can clip the amplitude flat with a limiter and throw amplitude noise away (L5).

DerivationThe spectrum of tone FM

  1. Let \(m(t)=A_m\cos\omega_mt\). Integrate:

    \[ 2\pi k_f\!\int A_m\cos\omega_m\tau\,d\tau=\frac{k_fA_m}{f_m}\sin\omega_mt=\beta\sin\omega_mt,\qquad \beta=\frac{\Delta f}{f_m} \]
  2. \[ s(t)=A_c\cos(\omega_ct+\beta\sin\omega_mt)=\mathrm{Re}\{A_c\,e^{j\omega_ct}\,e^{j\beta\sin\omega_mt}\} \]

    Why complex: the hard part, \(e^{j\beta\sin\omega_mt}\), is periodic in \(t\) with period \(1/f_m\), so it has a Fourier series.

  3. Its Fourier coefficients are, by definition, Bessel functions of the first kind:

    \[ e^{j\beta\sin x}=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(\beta)\,e^{jnx},\qquad J_n(\beta)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{j(\beta\sin x-nx)}dx \]

  4. Substitute and take the real part:

    \[ s(t)=A_c\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(\beta)\cos\big[(\omega_c+n\omega_m)t\big] \]

    Read it: a carrier line \(J_0(\beta)\) and infinitely many sideband pairs at \(f_c\pm nf_m\), with amplitudes \(J_n(\beta)\). FM is non-linear: one tone gives many lines, unlike AM's two.

  5. Power is constant. Use the identity \(\sum_n J_n^2(\beta)=1\):

    \[ P=\frac{A_c^2}{2}\sum_nJ_n^2(\beta)=\frac{A_c^2}{2} \]

    Meaning: modulation only redistributes the unmodulated carrier's power among the lines. When \(J_0(\beta)=0\) (β = 2.405, 5.520, 8.654…) all of it is in the sidebands.

  6. Bandwidth. \(J_n(\beta)\) becomes tiny once \(n>\beta+1\). Keeping \(\beta+1\) pairs gives Carson's rule, about 98 % of the power:

    \[ B_T\approx2(\beta+1)f_m=2(\Delta f+f_m)\quad\text{general: }2(\Delta f+W) \]

    Stricter "1 % rule": keep every pair with \(|J_n|\ge0.01\); used for adjacent-channel planning.

  7. Narrowband FM (\(\beta\ll1\)). Use \(\cos(\beta\sin x)\approx1\), \(\sin(\beta\sin x)\approx\beta\sin x\):

    \[ s(t)\approx A_c\cos\omega_ct-\beta A_c\sin\omega_mt\,\sin\omega_ct \]

    Compare with AM: same carrier, same two sidebands, same \(B_T=2f_m\), but the sidebands are in quadrature with the carrier. That is why the amplitude stays (almost) constant.

Block diagramBuilding FM indirectly: the Armstrong transmitter

Press Next to build the system one block at a time, the same order as the lecture slides. Each step lights up a block and the scope trace it produces.

Swipe the diagram sideways to see the whole chain.

Why integrate, then phase-modulate?

Phase-modulating ∫m(t) gives exactly FM of m(t) (L6). A narrowband phase modulator built around a crystal oscillator keeps the carrier rock-steady, which a free-running VCO cannot.

Why multiply, then mix?

A × n multiplier multiplies both the carrier and the deviation: Δf₁ = 25 Hz × 3000 = 75 kHz. The mixer then moves the centre to the wanted fc without changing Δf.

InteractiveWatch the Bessel lines grow

Try Δf = 2.4 kHz with f_m = 1 kHz: the carrier line disappears (J₀(2.405) = 0). Then raise f_m with Δf fixed and watch β fall and the spectrum narrow.

Worked examplesFrom broadcast FM to Bessel tables

Example 1 · Broadcast FM bandwidth Carson
Given: \(\Delta f=75\) kHz, highest audio \(W=15\) kHz (mono).

\(D=75/15=5\); \(B_T=2(75+15)=180\) kHz. The 200 kHz channel raster leaves a 20 kHz guard.

Answer: D = 5, B_T = 180 kHz.

Example 2 · Carson vs the 1 % rule β = 5
Given: \(f_m=1\) kHz, \(\Delta f=5\) kHz.

Carson: \(2(5+1)=12\) kHz (6 pairs). Power in those lines: \(J_0^2+2\sum_{n=1}^{6}J_n^2=0.9936\): 99.4 %.

1 % rule: \(J_8(5)=0.0184\ge0.01\) but \(J_9(5)=0.0055\), so 8 pairs: \(B=16\) kHz.

Answer: 12 kHz (Carson, 99.4 % of power) or 16 kHz (1 % rule).

Example 3 · Where the power goes β = 1
Given: \(A_c=10\) V into 50 Ω, \(\beta=1\).

Total \(P=10^2/(2\cdot50)=1\) W. Carrier \(J_0^2=0.5855\) W; first pair \(2J_1^2=0.387\) W; second pair \(2J_2^2=0.026\) W; the rest ≈ 0.001 W.

Answer: 58.6 % carrier, 38.7 % first pair, 2.6 % second pair.

Example 4 · Calibrating a transmitter carrier null
Given: a 1 kHz test tone; raise the audio level until the carrier line on a spectrum analyser first vanishes.

First zero of \(J_0\) is \(\beta=2.405\Rightarrow\Delta f=2.405\times1\ \text{kHz}=2.405\) kHz. Knowing the audio voltage at that point gives \(k_f\).

Answer: Δf = 2.405 kHz at the first carrier null: the Crosby/Bessel-null method.

Example 5 · From k_f to bandwidth design
Given: \(k_f=50\) kHz/V, \(m(t)=2\cos(2\pi\,2000t)\).

\(\Delta f=50\times2=100\) kHz; \(\beta=100/2=50\); \(B_T=2(100+2)=204\) kHz.

Answer: β = 50 (wideband), B_T ≈ 204 kHz.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Thinking FM bandwidth is \(2\Delta f\). Carson adds the message bandwidth: \(2(\Delta f+W)\).
  • Calling β the deviation. β is dimensionless (deviation ÷ message frequency); Δf is in Hz.
  • Expecting FM power to depend on the message. Total power is always \(A_c^2/2\).
