Lecture 5 · M1 Analog Modulation · CO1

Reading the frequency: discriminators, PLLs and FM's noise advantage

Drive under a power line with the AM radio on and you hear buzzing. Switch to FM and the music stays clean. FM spends extra bandwidth to buy a 20 dB quieter output: here is the derivation.

Derive the slope/differentiator discriminatorExplain the PLL as an FM demodulatorShow FM output noise is parabolicCompute FM's SNR gain, pre-emphasis and threshold
⏱ 50 minBTL-4 Analyse · BTL-5 Evaluate

ConceptA frequency detector turns Hz into volts

An FM demodulator must output a voltage proportional to \(f_i(t)-f_c=k_fm(t)\). Three classic ways:

Discriminator

Differentiate, so frequency becomes amplitude, then envelope-detect. Hardware: slope, balanced (Foster–Seeley), ratio detector.

Quadrature / I-Q

Compute the phase of the complex baseband sample by sample and take its difference. This is what GNU Radio's WBFM Receive does.

Phase-locked loop

A VCO is forced to track the incoming frequency; the control voltage that keeps it locked is the message.

Every FM receiver puts a limiter before the detector: it clips the amplitude flat so that amplitude noise (the power-line buzz) cannot get through. Only the zero crossings, which carry the frequency, survive.

Analogy: the dancer and the mirrorIn a PLL the VCO is a dancer copying a partner (the incoming signal). If the partner speeds up, the dancer must push harder to keep up. Measure how hard the dancer pushes (the control voltage) and you know how the partner's speed changed: the message.

Block diagramInside an FM receiver: block by block

Press Next to build the system one block at a time, the same order as the lecture slides. Each step lights up a block and the scope trace it produces.

Swipe the diagram sideways to see the whole chain.

Limiter first

It clips the amplitude flat and a filter restores a clean sine. Amplitude noise (ignition, power-line buzz) is removed, while the zero crossings, which carry the frequency, are kept.

Discriminator = d/dt + envelope detector

d/dt turns frequency into amplitude: the envelope becomes Ac[ωc + 2πkf m(t)]. An ordinary envelope detector reads it, and a DC block removes Acωc, leaving m(t).

DerivationDetectors and the noise advantage

A · The differentiator discriminator

  1. Start from \(s(t)=A_c\cos\theta(t)\) with \(\theta'(t)=\omega_c+2\pi k_fm(t)\). Differentiate:

    \[ \frac{ds}{dt}=-A_c\big[\omega_c+2\pi k_fm(t)\big]\sin\theta(t) \]

  2. This is an AM-like wave: a carrier \(\sin\theta(t)\) whose envelope is \(A_c[\omega_c+2\pi k_fm(t)]\), always positive since \(\omega_c\gg2\pi\Delta f\).

    \[ \text{envelope detector}\;\Rightarrow\;y(t)=A_c\omega_c+2\pi k_fA_c\,m(t) \]

    Why the limiter matters: the output scales with \(A_c\). Any amplitude fluctuation would leak into the audio, so the limiter fixes \(A_c\) first. A DC block removes \(A_c\omega_c\).

B · The PLL demodulator

  1. The VCO output frequency is \(f_c+k_v\,v(t)\), with \(k_v\) in Hz/V. The phase detector compares input and VCO phase; the loop filter drives \(v(t)\) to cancel the error.

  2. When locked, the VCO frequency equals the input frequency:

    \[ f_c+k_vv(t)=f_c+k_fm(t)\quad\Rightarrow\quad v(t)=\frac{k_f}{k_v}\,m(t) \]

    Simplification: in lock the phase error is small, so \(\sin\phi_e\approx\phi_e\) and the loop is linear. The loop bandwidth must exceed W so the VCO can follow the message.

C · Why FM output noise is parabolic

  1. Add narrowband noise to a carrier of amplitude \(A_c\). For high carrier-to-noise ratio, only the noise component in quadrature with the carrier, \(n_Q(t)\), moves the phase:

    \[ \phi_n(t)\approx\frac{n_Q(t)}{A_c} \]

  2. The detector outputs frequency, the derivative of phase. Differentiation multiplies a spectrum by \(j2\pi f\), so the power spectrum by \(f^2\):

    \[ S_{f}(f)=\frac{f^2}{A_c^2}\,S_{n_Q}(f)=\frac{N_0f^2}{A_c^2},\quad |f|\le\frac{B_T}2 \]

    Picture: FM output noise is a parabola: quiet at low audio frequencies, loud at high ones. That is why pre-emphasis works (step 6).

  3. Integrate over the audio band \(|f|\le W\):

    \[ N_o=\int_{-W}^{W}\frac{N_0f^2}{A_c^2}\,df=\frac{2N_0W^3}{3A_c^2} \]

  4. Output signal power is \(k_f^2P_m\). With \(P_r=A_c^2/2\) and \(\gamma=P_r/(N_0W)\):

    \[ \text{SNR}_o=\frac{3k_f^2P_m}{W^2}\gamma\;\xrightarrow{\text{tone}}\;\frac32\beta^2\gamma \]

    The trade: output SNR grows as β², while bandwidth grows only as β. Doubling the deviation gives +6 dB SNR.

  5. Threshold. The approximation in step 1 needs a strong carrier. When the carrier-to-noise ratio in \(B_T\) falls below about 10 dB, noise occasionally spins the phase through 2π, the detector outputs "clicks", and SNR collapses. Above threshold FM wins; below it, AM can be better.

  6. Pre-emphasis / de-emphasis. Boost high audio frequencies before modulation with \(H_{pe}=1+jf/f_1\), cut them after detection with \(H_{de}=1/(1+jf/f_1)\). The message is unchanged, but the high-frequency part of the parabolic noise is cut. Improvement factor:

    \[ I=\frac{(W/f_1)^3}{3\left[W/f_1-\tan^{-1}(W/f_1)\right]},\qquad f_1=\frac1{2\pi\tau} \]

    Numbers: W = 15 kHz; τ = 50 µs (India, Europe) gives \(f_1=3.18\) kHz and I = 10.2 dB; τ = 75 µs (Americas) gives 13.2 dB.

Block diagramThe PLL demodulator: watch it lock

Press Next to build the system one block at a time, the same order as the lecture slides. Each step lights up a block and the scope trace it produces.

Swipe the diagram sideways to see the whole chain.

Phase detector + loop filter

The multiplier gives the phase difference between the input and the VCO, plus a 2fc term. The loop filter removes the 2fc term and leaves a slowly varying control voltage v(t).

Why v(t) is the message

Locked means fVCO = fin, so fc + kv v(t) = fc + kf m(t), giving v(t) = (kf / kv)·m(t). The voltage that keeps the VCO in step is the message itself.

InteractiveBuy SNR with bandwidth

Left: output SNR of each system for the same received power. Right: noise spectrum at the FM detector output (parabola) and after de-emphasis, W = 15 kHz.

Worked examplesQuantifying the advantage

Example 1 · FM vs AM at the same power figure of merit
Given: tone FM with β = 5; tone AM with μ = 1.

FM: \(\tfrac32\beta^2=37.5\Rightarrow+15.7\) dB. AM: \(1/3\Rightarrow-4.8\) dB.

Answer: FM is 20.5 dB better, at the cost of 12 kHz instead of 2 kHz per kHz of message (6×).

Example 2 · A broadcast receiver end-to-end SNR
Given: γ = 40 dB, β = 5 (tone), de-emphasis 50 µs.

Without de-emphasis: \(40+15.7=55.7\) dB. With de-emphasis: \(+10.2\) dB → about 65.9 dB.

Answer: ≈ 66 dB output SNR, hi-fi quality.

Example 3 · Doubling the deviation trade-off
Given: broadcast FM, W = 15 kHz, Δf raised from 75 to 150 kHz.

SNR: \(\beta^2\) ×4 → +6.0 dB. Bandwidth: \(2(75+15)=180\) kHz → \(2(150+15)=330\) kHz.

Answer: +6 dB SNR for 1.83× bandwidth.

Example 4 · PLL design VCO gain
Given: VCO gain \(k_v=10\) kHz/V, peak deviation 75 kHz.

\(v_{peak}=\Delta f/k_v=75/10=7.5\) V. The loop must swing ±7.5 V and have bandwidth above 15 kHz.

Answer: ±7.5 V control voltage.

Example 5 · Above threshold? link check
Given: receiver noise figure 7 dB, \(B_T=180\) kHz, received carrier −90 dBm.

Noise: \(-174+10\log_{10}(180\,000)+7=-114.4\) dBm. CNR = −90 − (−114.4) = 24.4 dB, well above 10 dB.

Minimum carrier for threshold: −114.4 + 10 = −104.4 dBm.

Answer: CNR 24.4 dB, above threshold; threshold reached at about −104 dBm.

Phone FM chips

Capture effect

An FM receiver locks onto the stronger of two stations and suppresses the weaker: great for broadcast, risky for aviation.

PLLs everywhere

The same loop synthesises your phone's carrier, recovers clocks in USB and demodulates FM.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Claiming FM's advantage holds at any SNR. It needs the CNR above threshold (≈ 10 dB).
  • Forgetting the limiter: without it the discriminator also responds to amplitude noise.
  • Pre-emphasising at the receiver. Pre-emphasis is at the transmitter, de-emphasis at the receiver.

Quick checkThree questions

1. The limiter in an FM receiver removes

Information is in the frequency; the limiter flattens amplitude noise.

2. FM output noise PSD grows with audio frequency as

Frequency is the derivative of phase, so the noise PSD is multiplied by f².

3. Below threshold, FM output

Noise causes 2π phase slips that the discriminator turns into impulses.

Lecture 6 · M1 Analog Modulation · CO1

Phase modulation: FM's twin, and the parent of digital radio

Show a student the waveform \(10\cos(2\pi10^6t+3\sin2\pi2000t)\) and ask "FM or PM?". The honest answer is you cannot tell. This lecture shows why, and why the difference still matters.

Write the PM signal and its instantaneous frequencyConvert between FM and PM with an integrator/differentiatorCompare how β and bandwidth depend on f_mConnect PM to BPSK and QPSK
⏱ 50 minBTL-2 Understand · BTL-4 Analyse

ConceptLet the phase follow the message

\[ s_{PM}(t)=A_c\cos\big[2\pi f_ct+k_p\,m(t)\big] \]

\(k_p\) is the phase sensitivity in rad/V. The instantaneous frequency follows the slope of the message:

\[ f_i(t)=f_c+\frac{k_p}{2\pi}\,\frac{dm}{dt} \]

FM

Frequency ∝ m(t). Phase ∝ ∫m(t). A step in m makes a step in frequency.

PM

Phase ∝ m(t). Frequency ∝ dm/dt. A step in m makes a sudden jump in phase (and an impulse in frequency).

Analogy: two runners on a circular trackRunner FM changes speed whenever the coach (message) shouts. Runner PM is told where to be on the track; to get there she must sprint when the instructions change quickly and can stroll when they change slowly. Watch only the speed and you cannot tell which coach gave the orders.

DerivationOne family, two members

  1. Both are angle modulation \(s(t)=A_c\cos[\omega_ct+\psi(t)]\):

    \[ \psi_{FM}(t)=2\pi k_f\!\int_0^t\!m(\tau)d\tau,\qquad \psi_{PM}(t)=k_p\,m(t) \]

  2. FM from a PM modulator: integrate the message first, then phase-modulate with \(k_p=2\pi k_f\):

    \[ m(t)\to\boxed{\int}\to\boxed{\text{PM}}\;=\;\text{FM} \]

    History: the Armstrong transmitter does exactly this. A crystal oscillator is easy to phase-modulate slightly but hard to frequency-modulate stably.

  3. PM from an FM modulator: differentiate the message first:

    \[ m(t)\to\boxed{\tfrac{d}{dt}}\to\boxed{\text{FM}}\;=\;\text{PM} \]

  4. Tone PM. Let \(m(t)=A_m\sin\omega_mt\):

    \[ s(t)=A_c\cos(\omega_ct+\beta_p\sin\omega_mt),\qquad \beta_p=k_pA_m \]

    Same form as tone FM, so the same Bessel spectrum and Carson's rule apply, with β = β_p.

  5. Instantaneous frequency deviation:

    \[ \Delta f_{PM}=\frac{k_pA_m\omega_m}{2\pi}=\beta_p\,f_m \]
    \[ \text{FM: }\beta=\frac{k_fA_m}{f_m}\ (\Delta f\text{ fixed}),\qquad \text{PM: }\beta=k_pA_m\ (\Delta f\propto f_m) \]

    Consequence: in PM, high message frequencies produce large deviation and wide bandwidth. In FM, high frequencies get a small β and therefore worse noise performance, which pre-emphasis partly fixes (pre-emphasis makes FM behave like PM at high audio frequencies).

  6. Noise. A phase detector outputs phase, so its output noise PSD is flat (not parabolic):

    \[ \text{SNR}_{o,PM}=k_p^2P_m\,\gamma\;\xrightarrow{\text{tone}}\;\frac{\beta_p^2}{2}\gamma \]

    Comparison: FM gets \(\tfrac32\beta^2\gamma\), three times more for the same β, because its parabolic noise is mostly outside the low audio frequencies where the tone sits.

  7. Bridge to digital. Let \(m(t)\) take only two values with \(k_pm=0\) or \(\pi\): the carrier phase jumps by 180° per bit. That is BPSK. Four values (0, 90°, 180°, 270°) give QPSK, the modulation of Practical P4.

FMPM
Angle\(2\pi k_f\int m\)\(k_pm(t)\)
Instantaneous frequency\(f_c+k_fm(t)\)\(f_c+\frac{k_p}{2\pi}\dot m(t)\)
Tone index β\(k_fA_m/f_m\)\(k_pA_m\)
Peak deviation\(k_fA_m\) (fixed)\(\beta_pf_m\) (grows with f_m)
Output noise PSD∝ f² (parabolic)flat
Used inbroadcast, two-way radioArmstrong FM, PSK, QAM, GSM (GMSK)

Block diagramOne block turns FM into PM, and PM into FM

Press Next to build the system one block at a time, the same order as the lecture slides. Each step lights up a block and the scope trace it produces.

Swipe the diagram sideways to see the whole chain.

The one-block rule

PM of m(t) = FM of dm/dt.
FM of m(t) = PM of ∫m(t) dt.
A differentiator or an integrator is the only difference between the two transmitters.

How to tell them apart

With a single tone you cannot: both look the same. Change the message. A triangle gives a smooth sweep in FM but frequency jumps in PM; and raising fm leaves FM’s Δf fixed but grows PM’s Δf = kp·Am·fm.

Block diagramBuilding PM: the narrowband phase modulator

Press Next to build the system one block at a time, the same order as the lecture slides. Each step lights up a block and the scope trace it produces.

Swipe the diagram sideways to see the whole chain.

The trick: add a small quadrature term

cos(ωct + θ) = cos θ cos ωct − sin θ sin ωct ≈ cos ωct − θ sin ωct when |θ| ≪ 1 (say |θ| ≤ 0.2 rad). With θ = kp m(t), a multiplier, a 90° shift and an adder make PM.

Why it matters

Everything comes from one crystal oscillator, so the carrier is very stable. It is the first stage of the Armstrong FM transmitter (L4), and the same I/Q structure becomes the QPSK/QAM modulator of Module 2.

InteractiveSame message, FM vs PM

Triangle message: PM gives two frequencies (the slope is ± constant), exactly what FM does with a square message. Square message: PM shows sudden 180°-style phase jumps.

Worked examplesTelling the twins apart

Example 1 · Tone PM β and bandwidth
Given: \(k_p=2\) rad/V, \(m(t)=0.5\cos(2\pi1000t)\).

\(\beta=k_pA_m=1\) rad; \(\Delta f=\beta f_m=1\) kHz; \(B_T=2(1+1)=4\) kHz.

Answer: β = 1, Δf = 1 kHz, B_T = 4 kHz.

Example 2 · Raise the tone to 5 kHz FM vs PM
Given: the PM of Example 1, and an FM with the same Δf = 1 kHz at 1 kHz. Now f_m = 5 kHz.

PM: β stays 1, Δf = 5 kHz, \(B_T=2(5+5)=20\) kHz. FM: Δf stays 1 kHz, β = 0.2, \(B_T=2(1+5)=12\) kHz.

Answer: PM 20 kHz, FM 12 kHz. PM bandwidth grows with the message frequency.

Example 3 · PM of a triangle slope
Given: triangle rising 0 → 1 V in 0.5 ms; \(k_p=\pi\) rad/V.

Slope 2000 V/s. \(f_i-f_c=\dfrac{\pi}{2\pi}\cdot2000=1000\) Hz while rising, −1000 Hz while falling.

Answer: the carrier hops between f_c ± 1 kHz: binary FSK from an analog PM modulator.

Example 4 · FM of a square wave steps
Given: \(k_f=4\) kHz/V, square wave ±1 V.

\(f_i=f_c\pm4\) kHz, switching each half-period. This is FSK, the digital cousin.

Answer: f_c ± 4 kHz.

Example 5 · Which one is it? identification
Given: \(s(t)=10\cos(2\pi10^6t+3\sin2\pi2000t)\).

β = 3, \(\Delta f=3\times2=6\) kHz, \(B_T=2(6+2)=16\) kHz, power \(10^2/2=50\) W (1 Ω).

It could be FM of \(m=\cos\) with \(k_fA_m=6\) kHz, or PM of \(m=\sin\) with \(k_pA_m=3\) rad. Only changing \(f_m\) reveals which: FM keeps Δf, PM keeps β.

Answer: β = 3, Δf = 6 kHz, B_T = 16 kHz, P = 50 W; FM or PM is undecidable from one tone.

PracticeCheck yourself

Level 1

k_p = 3 rad/V, A_m = 0.5 V. Phase index β (rad)?

Level 2

Same PM at f_m = 2 kHz: peak frequency deviation in kHz?

Level 2

Carson bandwidth of that PM signal, in kHz?

Level 3

For the same tone β, how many dB better is FM's SNRₒ than PM's? (ratio 3)

Real worldPM is everywhere, under other names

GSM

GMSK, a smoothed phase modulation, carried 2G voice for billions of users.

Wi-Fi, LTE, 5G

QPSK and QAM change carrier phase (and amplitude) per symbol: digital PM.

Deep space

Spacecraft telemetry uses residual-carrier PM so Earth can lock a PLL onto the carrier.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Writing \(k_p\) in Hz/V. Phase sensitivity is in rad/V; frequency sensitivity \(k_f\) is in Hz/V.
  • Assuming PM deviation is fixed. It scales with the message frequency.
  • Thinking FM and PM need different receivers. A PLL or I-Q detector gives both: phase for PM, its derivative for FM.

SummaryFormula card

PM signal\(A_c\cos[\omega_ct+k_pm(t)]\)
Frequency\(f_c+\frac{k_p}{2\pi}\dot m\)
FM ⇄ PMFM = PM(∫m), PM = FM(ṁ)
Tone index\(\beta_p=k_pA_m\)
Deviation\(\Delta f=\beta_pf_m\)
PM SNR\(k_p^2P_m\gamma\)

2. To make FM with a phase modulator you first

Phase = 2πk_f∫m: integrate, then phase-modulate (Armstrong).

3. BPSK is PM with

Lecture 7 · M1 Analog Modulation · CO1

Real-world contexts: AM broadcast, FM broadcast and the airband

Every time a flight lands at Hyderabad, the pilot talks to the tower using the same AM as a 1920s radio. Every FM station hides a stereo signal and a data channel above your hearing. Let's read the spectrum like an engineer.

Recall the bands and channel plansExplain why each service chose AM or FMCompute channel counts and antenna sizesDecode the FM stereo multiplex
⏱ 50 minBTL-2 Understand · BTL-3 Apply

ConceptThree services, three design choices

AM broadcast (medium wave)FM broadcastAviation VHF voice
Band531–1602 kHz (India, ITU Region 3); 520/530–1700/1710 kHz (Americas)88–108 MHz (76–95 MHz in Japan)118–137 MHz
ModulationDSB-FC AMWideband FM, Δf = 75 kHzDSB-FC AM
Channel spacing9 kHz (India, Europe); 10 kHz (Americas)200 kHz raster (100 kHz steps in many countries)25 kHz; 8.33 kHz in Europe
Audio bandwidth≈ 4.5 kHz15 kHz, stereo≈ 3 kHz speech
PropagationGround wave by day, sky wave at night: hundreds of kmLine of sight: 50–100 kmLine of sight to aircraft at altitude: up to ~ 300 km
Why this choiceSimplest receivers, long reachHi-fi quality, noise immunityNo capture effect: overlapping calls are both heard; simple, robust
Why aviation stays with AMIf two pilots press "transmit" at once on FM, the stronger signal captures the receiver and the weaker one vanishes silently: the controller does not even know a call was missed. On AM both are heard as a squeal, so everyone knows to repeat. Safety beats audio quality.

DerivationThe FM stereo multiplex, step by step

FM stereo had to stay compatible with mono receivers. The solution is a baseband FDM signal that frequency-modulates the carrier:

  1. Form the sum and difference of the left and right channels:

    \[ M=L+R,\qquad S=L-R \]

    Compatibility: a mono receiver plays only M = L + R, which is complete mono audio.

  2. Put S on a 38 kHz DSB-SC sub-carrier, add a 19 kHz pilot at half that frequency, and (optionally) RDS data at 57 kHz:

    \[ x(t)=(L+R)+(L-R)\cos(2\pi\,38\text{k}\,t)+A_p\cos(2\pi\,19\text{k}\,t)+x_{RDS}(t) \]

  3. Spectrum of \(x(t)\): 0.03–15 kHz (L+R), pilot at 19 kHz, 23–53 kHz (L−R), RDS around 57 kHz. Highest frequency \(W\approx53\) kHz (≈ 60 kHz with RDS).

  4. The receiver doubles the pilot to regenerate the 38 kHz carrier in phase (coherent detection of DSB-SC, Lecture 3), recovers S, then

    \[ L=\tfrac12(M+S),\qquad R=\tfrac12(M-S) \]

  5. Bandwidth with Carson's rule:

    \[ B_T=2(\Delta f+W)=2(75+53)=256\ \text{kHz} \]

    Reality check: wider than the 200 kHz raster. Regulators avoid placing strong stations in adjacent channels in the same city, and most energy lies well inside Carson's band.

InteractiveExplore the radio spectrum

Tap a band on the logarithmic ruler to see its modulation, channel plan and the antenna size it needs.

Worked examplesChannel plans and hardware

Example 1 · How many AM stations fit? India
Given: 531–1602 kHz, 9 kHz spacing.

\(N=\dfrac{1602-531}{9}+1=119+1=120\) channels.

Answer: 120 channels (Americas: 530–1700 kHz at 10 kHz gives 118).

Example 2 · FM channels 200 kHz raster
Given: centres 88.1 … 107.9 MHz every 0.2 MHz.

\(N=\dfrac{107.9-88.1}{0.2}+1=99+1=100\).

Answer: 100 channels.

Example 3 · Airband capacity 8.33 kHz
Given: 118.000–136.975 MHz.

At 25 kHz: \(\dfrac{136.975-118}{0.025}+1=760\) channels. At 8.33 kHz each 25 kHz slot holds 3: 2280 channels.

Answer: 760 → 2280, which is why Europe's crowded airspace moved to 8.33 kHz.

Example 4 · Antennas for the three services λ/4
Given: 1 MHz, 100 MHz, 125 MHz.

\(L=75/f_{\text{MHz}}\): 75 m (MW mast), 0.75 m (car whip), 0.6 m (aircraft blade antenna).

Answer: 75 m, 75 cm, 60 cm.

Example 5 · AM power on air broadcast
Given: a 100 kW (carrier) MW transmitter, average programme modulation μ = 0.3.

\(P_t=100(1+0.09/2)=104.5\) kW. Information power: 4.5 kW (4.3 %).

Answer: 104.5 kW radiated, only 4.5 kW in the sidebands. A big reason for DRM digital radio.

Lecture 8 · First lab · M1 Analog Modulation · CO1

Your first radio: demodulate an FM station with an RTL-SDR and GNU Radio

A ₹2,500 USB dongle that was designed for TV can become a complete FM receiver. In this session you build it block by block and hear real music from the air through a flowgraph you made.

Install and test the RTL-SDRDesign the sample-rate chain 1.92 MS/s → 48 kHzBuild the flowgraph in GNU Radio CompanionMeasure the station bandwidth and audio quality
⏱ 2 h labBTL-3 Apply · BTL-6 CreateReceive only

ConceptWhat the dongle gives you

Hardware

  • RTL2832U demodulator chip + R820T2/R828D tuner (RTL-SDR Blog V3/V4 recommended)
  • Tuning range about 24 MHz – 1.766 GHz
  • 8-bit I/Q samples, up to 3.2 MS/s (2.4 MS/s is reliable)
  • Receive only: it cannot transmit, so it is completely safe to use

The idea

The tuner mixes the chosen frequency down to baseband and the chip delivers complex samples \(x[n]=I[n]+jQ[n]\). Everything after that (filtering, demodulation, de-emphasis, resampling) is the software you write. It is the receiver of Lectures 4 and 5, built from blocks.

What to expect: every spacing is a multiple of the channel raster, never less than about 200 kHz between neighbours in one city, and each station occupies about 180–200 kHz (Carson: 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz). In SDR++ set the WFM demodulator, 200 kHz bandwidth, and use the FFT zoom to read the peak frequency.

DesignPlan the sample rates and the tuning offset

  1. Capture rate. One FM station needs about 200 kHz; we want a little spectrum around it for the displays. Choose

    \[ f_s=1.92\ \text{MS/s} \]

    Why 1.92: it divides cleanly: \(1.92\text{M}/8=240\) k and \(240\text{k}/5=48\) k, the sound-card rate. No fractional resampler needed.

  2. Offset tuning. The dongle has a spike at its own centre frequency (DC offset, LO leakage). Tune the hardware 250 kHz above the station:

    \[ f_{LO}=f_{station}+250\ \text{kHz}\;\Rightarrow\;\text{station appears at }-250\ \text{kHz} \]

    Then shift it back to 0 Hz in software with the Frequency Xlating FIR Filter set to \(-250\) kHz.

  3. Channel filter and decimation by 8. Low-pass 100 kHz with a 25 kHz transition, then keep every 8th sample:

    \[ f_{s2}=\frac{1.92\ \text{M}}{8}=240\ \text{kS/s},\qquad \pm120\ \text{kHz}>\pm\frac{B_T}2=\pm90\ \text{kHz}\ \checkmark \]

  4. FM demodulation. WBFM Receive computes the phase difference of consecutive samples (the I-Q discriminator of Lecture 5), applies de-emphasis (fixed at 75 µs in the GRC block of GNU Radio 3.10; Indian stations use 50 µs, so the treble sounds slightly duller), and decimates by 5:

    \[ f_{audio}=\frac{240\ \text{k}}{5}=48\ \text{kHz} \]

  5. Check the discriminator range. Phase step per sample at peak deviation:

    \[ \Delta\theta=2\pi\frac{\Delta f}{f_{s2}}=2\pi\frac{75\ \text{k}}{240\ \text{k}}=1.96\ \text{rad}<\pi\ \checkmark \]

    Meaning: no phase wrapping, so the discriminator is unambiguous.

\[ 1.92\ \text{MS/s}\xrightarrow{\text{shift }-250\text{k},\ \text{LPF},\ \div8}240\ \text{kS/s}\xrightarrow{\text{WBFM},\ \div5}48\ \text{kHz}\to\text{speaker} \]The whole receiver in one line

ProcedureBuild it step by step

Stage 1 · Test the hardware (15 min)

  1. Plug in the dongle with the antenna fitted. Windows: run Zadig once, choose "Bulk-In, Interface (Interface 0)", install WinUSB. Linux: blacklist the TV driver: echo 'blacklist dvb_usb_rtl28xxu' | sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/rtl.conf, then replug.

  2. Open a Radioconda prompt or terminal and run rtl_test -t (should find the tuner) and SoapySDRUtil --find="driver=rtlsdr" (should list the device).

  3. Optional preview: open SDR++, select RTL-SDR, tune to 98.3 MHz in WFM mode. Note which stations are strongest in your room.

Stage 2 · Build the flowgraph (45 min)

  1. GNU Radio Companion → File → New → QT GUI. Save as m1_rtlsdr_fm.grc.

  2. Add every block in the table below with Ctrl+F, set the IDs and values exactly, and leave the rest at default.

  3. Make the connections, then Generate (F5) and Run (F6). Set freq to a strong station and raise gain until the station stands 30–40 dB above the noise floor without the floor itself rising.

Audio stutters, "aU" in consoleRates do not reach 48 kHz, or PC too slowCheck 1.92 M ÷ 8 ÷ 5 = 48 k; close other programs
Station a little off-centreCrystal error (ppm)Set Frequency Correction (PPM) in the source, typically 0–2 for V3/V4
Spike in the middle of the spectrumDC offset of the dongleThat is why we tune 250 kHz away; ignore it

Extend itTurn this into other receivers

Airband AM

Lecture 9 · Supplementary · CO1

Throw away the carrier, then throw away a sideband

Conventional AM spends at least two-thirds of its power on a carrier that carries nothing. Remove it and you save 66.7 % of the power; remove one sideband as well and you save 83.3 % and half the bandwidth.

Write DSB-SC, SSB and VSB in time and frequencyDerive the phase-shift SSB equationExplain the quadrature null and SSB phase distortionDraw the Costas loop
⏱ 50 minBTL-2 Understand · BTL-4 Analyse (suggested)

ConceptThree ways to spend less

DSB-SC

\(s(t)=A_c m(t)\cos\omega_c t\). No carrier, both sidebands. \(B_T=2W\), efficiency 100 %. The envelope is \(|m(t)|\), so an envelope detector fails: detection must be coherent.

SSB-SC

Only one sideband. \(B_T=W\), half of DSB. Used for HF voice and amateur radio, and in old telephone FDM.

VSB

One sideband plus a vestige of the other. Needed when the message has energy near DC (analog TV video). \(B_T=W+f_v\).

Analogy: the mirror imageThe two sidebands of DSB are mirror images of each other: every word is written twice. SSB keeps one copy. VSB keeps one copy plus the first few letters of the other, so the start of each word (the low frequencies) is not lost at the filter edge.

DerivationCoherent detection, SSB and the VSB condition

A · DSB-SC with a phase and frequency error

  1. Multiply \(s(t)=A_cm(t)\cos\omega_ct\) by the local oscillator \(\cos[(\omega_c+\Delta\omega)t+\phi]\):

    \[ v(t)=\tfrac{A_c}{2}m(t)\cos(\Delta\omega t+\phi)+\tfrac{A_c}{2}m(t)\cos\big((2\omega_c+\Delta\omega)t+\phi\big) \]

  2. Low-pass filter:

    \[ v_o(t)=\tfrac{A_c}{2}\,m(t)\cos(\Delta\omega t+\phi) \]

    Read it: a fixed phase error scales the output by \(\cos\phi\) (zero at 90°: the quadrature null); a frequency error makes it beat at \(\Delta f\).

B · The phase-shift (Hartley) SSB equation

  1. For a tone, DSB is

    \[A_m\cos\omega_mt\cos\omega_ct=\tfrac{A_m}{2}[\cos(\omega_c-\omega_m)t+\cos(\omega_c+\omega_m)t]\]

  2. Add a second DSB built from the 90°-shifted tone and carrier:

    \[A_m\sin\omega_mt\sin\omega_ct=\tfrac{A_m}{2}[\cos(\omega_c-\omega_m)t-\cos(\omega_c+\omega_m)t]\]

  3. Subtract to cancel the lower sideband, add to cancel the upper:

    \[ s_{SSB}(t)=\tfrac{A_c}{2}\big[m(t)\cos\omega_ct\mp\hat m(t)\sin\omega_ct\big] \]

    Hilbert transform \(\hat m(t)\) shifts every frequency component by −90°. Minus sign → USB, plus sign → LSB.

  4. Coherent detection of SSB with phase error \(\phi\):

    \[ v_o\propto m(t)\cos\phi\mp\hat m(t)\sin\phi \]

    Consequence: amplitude is kept but the waveform is phase-distorted ("Donald Duck" voice). The ear tolerates this better than DSB's fading.

The Weaver (third) method uses two stages of quadrature mixing and avoids the wideband 90° shifter, so it suits DSP and SDR.

C · VSB: the filter condition

  1. VSB = DSB-SC filtered by \(H(f)\). After coherent detection the output spectrum is

    \[\tfrac{A_c}{4}M(f)\,[H(f-f_c)+H(f+f_c)]\]

  2. For an undistorted message:

    \[ H(f-f_c)+H(f+f_c)=\text{constant},\qquad |f|\le W \]

    Meaning: the filter's roll-off is odd-symmetric about \(f_c\): what the vestige keeps of one sideband exactly fills what the cut removed from the other.

D · Costas loop: recovering the carrier

Two arms multiply the input by \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) of the VCO. After low-pass filtering, \(I\propto m(t)\cos\phi\), \(Q\propto m(t)\sin\phi\), and \(I\cdot Q\propto\tfrac12 m^2(t)\sin2\phi\) steers the VCO until \(\phi\to0\). No pilot needed.

Worked examplesVerified with experiment E2

Example 1 · Power saving DSB-SC, SSB
Given: an AM transmitter at μ = 1 radiates 1.5 kW. Find: the power saved by sending DSB-SC or SSB with the same sideband power.

\(P_c=1\) kW, \(P_{SB}=0.5\) kW. DSB-SC sends 0.5 kW → saving 66.7 %. SSB sends 0.25 kW → saving 83.3 %.

Answer: 66.7 % and 83.3 %.

Example 2 · Phase error coherent detector
Given: DSB-SC detected with φ = 0°, 30°, 60°, 90°.

Gain = cos φ = 1, 0.866, 0.5, 0. E2 measures exactly these values. SSB at 30° keeps amplitude but shows 4.8 dB of phase distortion.

Answer: 1, 0.866, 0.5, 0.

Example 3 · Occupied bandwidth two-tone message
Given: a message from 1 to 3 kHz on a 20 kHz carrier (E2).

DSB 17–23 kHz; USB 21–23 kHz; LSB 17–19 kHz; VSB with 2 kHz vestige 19–23 kHz.

Answer: 6, 2, 2 and 4 kHz.

Lecture 10 · Supplementary · CO1

Modulators: a diode, a transistor, a varactor and a lot of multiplication

A linear circuit can never create a new frequency. Every modulator therefore hides a non-linear or switching element, and every FM broadcast transmitter once hid a chain of frequency multipliers worth ×3072.

Derive the square-law and switching modulatorsExplain balanced and ring modulatorsSize a varactor VCOTrace an Armstrong transmitter
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply · BTL-6 Create (suggested)

ConceptGenerating AM and DSB-SC

ModulatorPrincipleOutputCircuit in this module
Square-law\(i=a_1v+a_2v^2\); band-pass at \(f_c\)AM, \(k_a=2a_2/a_1\)C10 (educational)
SwitchingLarge carrier switches a diode: \(\times g_p(t)\)AM, \(k_a=4/\pi A_c\)—
Balanced / diode ringTwo AM modulators fed with ±m(t), subtracted; ring = polarity switchDSB-SCC06 (verified)
Gilbert cell (AD633)\(W=(X_1-X_2)(Y_1-Y_2)/10\,\text{V}+Z\)DSB-SC (Z = 0) or AM (Z = carrier)C12 (educational)
Collector, class CSupply \(V_{CC}+m(t)\) sets output amplitudeHigh-level AMC11 (educational)

DerivationSquare-law, balanced and Armstrong

A · Square-law modulator

  1. Apply \(v=A_c\cos\omega_ct+m(t)\) to a device with \(i=a_1v+a_2v^2\):

    \[ i=a_1A_c\Big[1+\tfrac{2a_2}{a_1}m(t)\Big]\cos\omega_ct+a_1m(t)+a_2m^2(t)+a_2A_c^2\cos^2\omega_ct \]

  2. A band-pass filter at \(f_c\), width \(2W\), keeps only the first term: AM with \(k_a=2a_2/a_1\).

    Condition: \(f_c>3W\), so the \(m^2(t)\) term (up to \(2W\)) does not overlap the band.

B · Balanced modulator

  1. \[ s_1-s_2=A_c[1+k_am]\cos\omega_ct-A_c[1-k_am]\cos\omega_ct=2k_aA_c\,m(t)\cos\omega_ct \]

    Result: the carrier cancels, the sidebands double: DSB-SC.

C · Direct FM with a varactor

  1. Reverse-biased varactor: \(C_v(V)=\dfrac{C_{j0}}{(1+V/\phi)^m}\), \(m\approx0.5\) for an abrupt junction.

  2. Oscillator frequency \(f=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\). For small changes:

    \[ \frac{\Delta f}{f_0}\approx-\frac12\,\frac{\Delta C}{C_0} \]

D · Indirect (Armstrong) FM

  1. Integrate the message and make narrowband PM on a crystal carrier \(f_1\): this is NBFM with a tiny, linear \(\Delta f_1\).

  2. A ×n multiplier multiplies both \(f_c\) and \(\Delta f\) by n. A mixer moves \(f_c\) and leaves \(\Delta f\) alone.

  3. Haykin & Moher's example: \(f_1=200\) kHz, \(\Delta f_1=25\) Hz → ×64 → 12.8 MHz, 1.6 kHz → mix with 10.9 MHz → 1.9 MHz, 1.6 kHz → ×48 →

    \[ f_c=91.2\ \text{MHz},\qquad \Delta f=76.8\ \text{kHz} \]
Direct (VCO)Indirect (Armstrong)
StabilityNeeds AFC / PLLCrystal-stable
DeviationLarge, directlySmall, then multiplied
LinearityLimited by varactor lawGood
TodayPLL synthesiser + VCOHistorical; I/Q or DDS in SDRs

Worked examplesDesign numbers

Example 1 · Square-law index AM
Given: \(a_1=10\) mA/V, \(a_2=2\) mA/V², carrier 1 V, \(m(t)=0.5\cos\omega_mt\).

\(k_a=2a_2/a_1=0.4\ \text{V}^{-1}\), \(\mu=k_aA_m=0.2\).

Answer: μ = 0.2.

Example 2 · VCO capacitance direct FM
Given: 10.7 MHz VCO with \(L=2.2\) µH; want \(\Delta f=75\) kHz.

\(C=1/((2\pi\cdot10.7\text{M})^2\cdot2.2\mu)=100.6\) pF; \(\Delta C\approx2C\Delta f/f=1.41\) pF.

Answer: 100.6 pF, ±1.41 pF.

Example 3 · Colpitts at 10.7 MHz oscillator
Given: \(L=1\) µH, \(C_1=C_2\).

\(C_{eq}=221\) pF → \(C_1=C_2=442\) pF. With standard 470 pF: \(C_{eq}=235\) pF → 10.38 MHz; trim. (C04 at 1 MHz verified in ngspice: 1.032 MHz vs 1.038 MHz theory.)

Answer: 442 pF each; 10.38 MHz with 470 pF.

Lecture 11 · Supplementary · CO1

One fixed IF for every station, and a ghost station called the image

Tune an MW radio to 1000 kHz and a station at 1910 kHz comes out of the mixer at exactly the same 455 kHz. Nothing after the mixer can tell them apart.

Find LO and image frequenciesCompute image rejection (IFRR)Explain LO trackingDesign a second-order PLL
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply · BTL-5 Evaluate (suggested)

ConceptWhy the superheterodyne won

A tuned-radio-frequency (TRF) receiver filters at the station frequency, so its bandwidth \(f/Q\) changes across the band: with Q = 100 it is 5.4 kHz at 540 kHz but 16.5 kHz at 1650 kHz. The superheterodyne mixes every station down to one fixed intermediate frequency (455 kHz for AM, 10.7 MHz for FM), where all the selectivity and gain are built once.

DerivationImage, IFRR, tracking and the PLL

  1. The mixer output contains \(f_{LO}\pm f_{RF}\); the IF filter keeps the difference. With the LO above the signal:

    \[ f_{LO}=f_s+f_{IF},\qquad f_{si}=f_{LO}+f_{IF}=f_s+2f_{IF} \]

  2. Only a pre-selector before the mixer can reject \(f_{si}\). A single tuned circuit of loaded Q attenuates it by

    \[ \alpha=\sqrt{1+Q^2\rho^2},\qquad \rho=\frac{f_{si}}{f_s}-\frac{f_s}{f_{si}} \]

    Two identical stages: multiply the α values (add the dB).

  3. Why the LO is above. For 540–1650 kHz and 455 kHz IF: LO above = 995–2105 kHz (ratio 2.116, capacitance ratio 4.48); LO below = 85–1195 kHz (ratio 14.1, capacitance ratio ≈ 198, impossible with a gang capacitor). Padder and trimmer capacitors keep the RF and LO sections tracking.

  4. Direct conversion. Make \(f_{LO}=f_s\) and use I and Q mixers: the image problem disappears. This is the architecture of the RTL-SDR in Lecture 8.

The phase-locked loop

  1. Phase detector (gain \(K_d\) V/rad) → loop filter \(F(s)\) → VCO (gain \(K_o\) rad/s/V). Loop gain \(K=K_dK_o\).

  2. First-order loop, frequency offset \(\Delta\omega\):

    \[ \sin\theta_e=\frac{\Delta\omega}{K},\qquad \text{hold-in range }|\Delta\omega|\le K \]

  3. PI loop filter \(F(s)=K_p+K_i/s\) gives a second-order loop:

    \[ \omega_n^2=KK_i,\qquad 2\zeta\omega_n=KK_p,\qquad t_s\approx\frac{4}{\zeta\omega_n} \]

    As an FM demodulator: in lock the VCO follows the input, so the control voltage is \(k_fm(t)/k_v\).

Worked examplesVerified with E7, G6 and E8

Example 1 · Image rejection Q = 100
Given: \(f_s=1000\) kHz, \(f_{IF}=455\) kHz, Q = 100.

\(f_{si}=1910\) kHz; \(\rho=1.91-0.5236=1.3864\); \(\alpha=\sqrt{1+138.6^2}=138.6\).

Answer: 42.8 dB.

Example 2 · Simulation check E7

An equally strong 1910 kHz station: without a pre-selector the desired-to-image ratio is 1.1 dB; Q = 20 gives 29.9 dB (theory 28.9); Q = 60 gives 39.4 dB (theory 38.4). In GNU Radio (G6, scaled frequencies): −1.4 dB off, 61.4 dB on.

Example 3 · First-order PLL lock
Given: \(K_d=0.5\) V/rad, \(K_o=2\pi\times20\) kHz/V, input 5 kHz off.

\(K=62\,832\ \text{s}^{-1}\) (10 kHz); \(\sin\theta_e=0.5\Rightarrow\theta_e=30^\circ\); hold-in ±10 kHz.

Answer: 30°, ±10 kHz.

Example 4 · Second-order PLL E8
Given: \(K_d=1\) V/rad, \(k_v=5\) kHz/V, \(f_n=2\) kHz, ζ = 0.707.

\(K=31\,416\), \(K_p=2\zeta\omega_n/K=0.5656\), \(K_i=\omega_n^2/K=5026.55\). A 1 kHz step settles in 0.37 ms (theory ≈ 0.45 ms) with zero phase error; as an FM demodulator the gain is 0.303 (theory 0.300).

C06Diode-ring balanced modulator verified in ngspice

Values: 4 × 1N4148, 1 mH : 2 × 0.25 mH

Result: USB 0.106 V, LSB 0.103 V, carrier −91 dB (ideal)

ngspice netlist copy and run
* c06_ring

.model D1N4148 D(IS=2.52n RS=0.568 N=1.752 CJO=4p M=0.4 TT=20n BV=100)
.model Q2N3904 NPN(IS=6.734f XTI=3 EG=1.11 VAF=74.03 BF=416.4 NE=1.259 ISE=6.734f IKF=66.78m XTB=1.5 BR=.7371 NC=2 ISC=0 IKR=0 RC=1 CJC=3.638p MJC=.3085 VJC=.75 FC=.5 CJE=4.493p MJE=.2593 VJE=.75 TR=239.5n TF=301.2p ITF=.4 VTF=4 XTF=2 RB=10)
.model VAR D(IS=1e-14 CJO=40p VJ=0.7 M=0.5 BV=30)


Vm m 0 SIN(0 0.3 5k)
Rsm m p1 50
Vc c 0 SIN(0 2 100k)
Rsc c ct1 50
* input transformer T1: primary p1-0, secondary a-b with centre tap ct1-equivalent: use two coupled halves
Lp1 p1 0 1m
Ls1a a ct1 0.25m
Ls1b ct1 b 0.25m
K1a Lp1 Ls1a 0.999
K1b Lp1 Ls1b 0.999
K1c Ls1a Ls1b 0.999
* ring
D1 a c2 D1N4148
D2 c2 b D1N4148
D3 b d2 D1N4148
D4 d2 a D1N4148
* output transformer T2: primary halves c2-ct2-d2 with centre tap grounded via Vc return
Lp2a c2 ct2 0.25m
Lp2b ct2 d2 0.25m
Ls2 o 0 1m
K2a Lp2a Ls2 0.999
K2b Lp2b Ls2 0.999
K2c Lp2a Lp2b 0.999
Rct ct2 0 1
Ro o 0 1k
.tran 0.1u 3m 0 0.1u
.control
run
wrdata /tmp/outputs/m1pkg/spice/c06_ring.dat v(o)
.endc
.end

Lecture 13 · GNU Radio 3.10 · CO1

Seven flowgraphs, every parameter spelled out

All seven compile with grcc 3.10.9.2; G3–G6 were run headless and measured. G7 is the RTL-SDR receiver from Lecture 8.

Exact block namesParameters in greenMeasured results.grc source to copy

How to useBuild or open

Either copy the .grc source into a file and open it in GNU Radio Companion, or build it: press Ctrl+F in the block tree, type the exact block name from the table, drag it in, set only the listed parameters. Blue ports carry complex samples, orange ports carry floats.

LabAfter lectureRun
1L3G1, G2 with E1, E2
2L11G6 with E3, E7
3L4, L8G3, G7 with E4
4L6G4, G5 with E5, E6, E8

    file_format: 1
    grc_version: 3.10.9.2

G4FM demodulation: quadrature vs PLL

m1_fm_demod.grc · Verified: Gain 0.99 (quadrature), 0.989 (PLL); SNR 45.6 / 44.9 dB at noise 0.3.

Block (Ctrl+F name)IDParameters to set
Importimport_0Import = import math
Variablesamp_rateValue = 240e3
VariablefmValue = 1000
VariabledfValue = 5000
QT GUI RangenoiseDefault Value = 0; Stop = 1; Step = 0.01
Signal SourcemessageFrequency = fm
Frequency Modanalog_frequency_modulator_fc_0Sensitivity = 2*math.pi*df/samp_rate
Noise Sourceanalog_noise_source_x_0Amplitude = noise; Seed = 5
Addchanneldefault
Throttleblocks_throttle2_0default
Low Pass Filterif_filterFIR Type = fir_filter_ccf; Cutoff Freq = df+fm; Transition Width = 2000
Quadrature Demodanalog_quadrature_demod_cf_0Gain = samp_rate/(2*math.pi*df)
Low Pass Filteraudio_lpfFIR Type = fir_filter_fff; Cutoff Freq = 1500; Transition Width = 500
PLL Frequency Detectoranalog_pll_freqdet_cf_0Loop Bandwidth = 2*math.pi*3000/samp_rate; Min Phase/sample = -2*math.pi*20e3/samp_rate; Max Phase/sample = 2*math.pi*20e3/samp_rate
Multiply Constpll_scaleConstant = samp_rate/(2*math.pi*df)

QT GUI Time Sinkqtgui_time_sink_x_0Name = "message, discriminator, PLL"; Number of Points = 1200; Y min = -1.5; Y max = 1.5; Number of Inputs = 3; Line 1 Label = "message"; Line 2 Label = "quadrature demod"; Line 3 Label = "PLL freq det"

metadata:
    file_format: 1
    grc_version: 3.10.9.2

G7FM broadcast receiver with an RTL-SDR

m1_rtlsdr_fm.grc · Verified: Compiles; live audio needs an RTL-SDR dongle.

Block (Ctrl+F name)IDParameters to set
Variablesamp_rateValue = 1.92e6
VariableoffsetValue = 250e3
QT GUI RangefreqDefault Value = 98.3e6; Start = 88e6; Stop = 108e6; Step = 100e3
QT GUI RangegainDefault Value = 30; Stop = 49.6; Step = 0.1
QT GUI RangevolumeDefault Value = 0.5; Stop = 1; Step = 0.05
Soapy RTLSDR Sourcesoapy_rtlsdr_source_0Center Freq (Hz) = freq + offset; RF Gain = gain
Frequency Xlating FIR Filterfreq_xlating_fir_filter_xxx_0Decimation = 8; Taps = firdes.low_pass(1, samp_rate, 100e3, 25e3); Center Frequency = -offset
WBFM Receiveanalog_wfm_rcv_0Quadrature Rate = samp_rate/8; Audio Decimation = 5
Multiply Constblocks_multiply_const_vxx_0Constant = volume
Audio Sinkaudio_sink_0Sample Rate = 48000
QT GUI Frequency Sinkqtgui_freq_sink_x_0Center Frequency (Hz) = freq + offset; Average = 0.2
QT GUI Waterfall Sinkqtgui_waterfall_sink_x_0Center Frequency (Hz) = freq + offset
QT GUI Frequency Sinkqtgui_freq_sink_x_1Name = "Audio spectrum"; Bandwidth (Hz) = 48000; Average = 0.2
GNU Radio Companion editor screenshot 3.10.9

Python · e1_am.py numpy, matplotlib
"""E1  Conventional AM: waveform, two-sided spectrum, modulation index and power (Module 1, CO1).
Requires: Python 3.9+, numpy, matplotlib.   Run: python e1_am.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 400e3                      # sample rate (Hz)
T = 0.02                        # 20 ms of signal (an integer number of periods)
t = np.arange(int(fs*T)) / fs
Ac, fc, fm, Am = 1.0, 20e3, 1e3, 1.0   # carrier amplitude/frequency, message frequency/amplitude
m = Am*np.cos(2*np.pi*fm*t)            # message (tone)

def two_sided(x):
    """Two-sided amplitude spectrum: each line shows the amplitude of that complex exponential."""
    X = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft(x)) / len(x)
    f = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fftfreq(len(x), 1/fs))
    return f, np.abs(X)

print(f"{'mu':>5s} {'Pc(theory)':>11s} {'Pt(theory)':>11s} {'Pt(meas)':>10s} {'eta %':>7s} {'SB line':>9s} {'SB theory':>10s}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(11, 8))
for row, mu in enumerate([0.5, 1.0, 1.5]):
    s = Ac*(1 + mu*m/Am)*np.cos(2*np.pi*fc*t)        # s(t) = Ac[1 + mu m_n(t)] cos(wc t)
    Pc = Ac**2/2                                       # carrier power (1-ohm load)
    Pt_th = Pc*(1 + mu**2/2)                           # total power, theory
    Pt_meas = np.mean(s**2)                            # total power, measured from samples
    eta = mu**2/(2 + mu**2)*100                        # efficiency
    f, S = two_sided(s)
    k = np.argmin(abs(f - (fc + fm)))                  # upper-sideband line (positive frequency)
    print(f"{mu:5.2f} {Pc:11.4f} {Pt_th:11.4f} {Pt_meas:10.4f} {eta:7.2f} {S[k]:9.4f} {mu*Ac/4:10.4f}")
    n = int(2/fm*fs)                                   # two message periods
    ax[row, 0].plot(t[:n]*1e3, s[:n], lw=0.8)
    ax[row, 0].plot(t[:n]*1e3, Ac*(1 + mu*m[:n]), 'r--', lw=1.2)   # envelope
    ax[row, 0].set(title=f'AM, μ = {mu}', xlabel='t (ms)', ylabel='s(t)')
    ax[row, 1].stem(f/1e3, S, markerfmt=' ', basefmt=' ')
    ax[row, 1].set(xlim=(-25, 25), title='Two-sided spectrum |S(f)|', xlabel='f (kHz)')
for a in ax.flat: a.grid(alpha=.4)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('e1_am.png', dpi=110)

# mu from the envelope (oscilloscope method) for mu = 0.5
s = Ac*(1 + 0.5*m)*np.cos(2*np.pi*fc*t)
env = Ac*(1 + 0.5*m)
mu_est = (env.max() - env.min())/(env.max() + env.min())
print(f"\nEnvelope method: Amax = {env.max():.3f}, Amin = {env.min():.3f}, mu = {mu_est:.3f}")
print(f"Bandwidth B = 2 fm = {2*fm/1e3:.1f} kHz; lines at {fc/1e3-fm/1e3:.0f}, {fc/1e3:.0f}, {fc/1e3+fm/1e3:.0f} kHz (and their negatives)")
plt.show()

Python · e2_dsb_ssb_vsb.py numpy, matplotlib
"""E2  DSB-SC, SSB (phase-shift method) and VSB; coherent detection with phase error.
Requires: numpy, matplotlib."""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 400e3; T = 0.02; t = np.arange(int(fs*T))/fs
fc = 20e3
m = 0.6*np.cos(2*np.pi*1e3*t) + 0.4*np.cos(2*np.pi*3e3*t)       # two-tone message, W = 3 kHz

def hilbert(x):
    """Hilbert transform via FFT: multiply positive frequencies by -j, negative by +j."""
    X = np.fft.fft(x); f = np.fft.fftfreq(len(x))
    return np.real(np.fft.ifft(X*(-1j*np.sign(f))))

def lpf(x, fcut):
    """Ideal (brick-wall) low-pass filter applied in the frequency domain."""
    X = np.fft.fft(x); f = np.fft.fftfreq(len(x), 1/fs); X[np.abs(f) > fcut] = 0
    return np.real(np.fft.ifft(X))

def spec(x):
    X = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft(x))/len(x); f = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fftfreq(len(x), 1/fs)); return f, np.abs(X)

c = np.cos(2*np.pi*fc*t); sn = np.sin(2*np.pi*fc*t)
dsb = m*c                                   # DSB-SC
usb = m*c - hilbert(m)*sn                   # SSB, upper sideband (Hartley)
lsb = m*c + hilbert(m)*sn                   # SSB, lower sideband
# VSB: keep USB fully and a vestige of the LSB with a filter that is antisymmetric around fc (here a linear ramp of +-1.5 kHz)
X = np.fft.fft(dsb); f = np.fft.fftfreq(len(t), 1/fs); af = np.abs(f)
H = np.clip((af - (fc - 1.5e3))/3e3, 0, 1)  # H(fc - x) + H(fc + x) = 1 for |x| < 1.5 kHz
vsb = np.real(np.fft.ifft(X*H))*2

def coherent(s, phi=0.0):
    return lpf(2*s*np.cos(2*np.pi*fc*t + phi), 5e3)

def snr_db(y, ref):
    g = np.dot(y, ref)/np.dot(ref, ref); e = y - g*ref
    return 10*np.log10(np.sum((g*ref)**2)/np.sum(e**2)), g

print(f"{'signal':>8s} {'power':>8s} {'occupied band (kHz)':>22s} {'recovered SNR (dB)':>20s} {'gain':>6s}")
for name, s, k in (('DSB-SC', dsb, 1), ('USB', usb, 2), ('LSB', lsb, 2), ('VSB', vsb, 1)):
    fx, Sx = spec(s); pos = (fx > 0) & (Sx > 1e-3); band = (fx[pos].min()/1e3, fx[pos].max()/1e3)
    y = coherent(s); q, g = snr_db(y, m)
    print(f"{name:>8s} {np.mean(s**2):8.4f} {band[0]:10.1f} – {band[1]:5.1f} {('> 100 (exact)' if q > 100 else f'{q:.1f}'):>20s} {g:6.2f}")

print('\nPhase error in the coherent DSB-SC detector:')
for deg in (0, 30, 60, 90):
    y = coherent(dsb, np.radians(deg)); g = np.dot(y, m)/np.dot(m, m)
    print(f"  phi = {deg:2d} deg: output gain = {g:6.3f}  (cos phi = {np.cos(np.radians(deg)):.3f})")
print('SSB with 30 deg phase error: amplitude kept, but phase distortion (Hilbert component leaks):')
y = coherent(usb, np.radians(30)); q, g = snr_db(y, m); print(f"  recovered 'SNR' vs m(t) = {q:.1f} dB (distortion, not noise)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 6))
for a, (name, s) in zip(ax.flat, (('DSB-SC', dsb), ('SSB (USB)', usb), ('SSB (LSB)', lsb), ('VSB', vsb))):
    fx, Sx = spec(s); a.stem(fx/1e3, Sx, markerfmt=' ', basefmt=' '); a.set(xlim=(-26, 26), title=name + ': two-sided spectrum', xlabel='f (kHz)'); a.grid(alpha=.4)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('e2_dsb_ssb_vsb.png', dpi=110)
plt.show()
MATLAB · e2_dsb_ssb_vsb.m no toolboxes; runs in Octave
% E2  DSB-SC, SSB (phase-shift method) and VSB; coherent detection with phase error. Core MATLAB.
clear; clc; close all;
fs = 400e3; T = 0.02; t = (0:round(fs*T)-1)/fs; N = numel(t);
fc = 20e3; m = 0.6*cos(2*pi*1e3*t) + 0.4*cos(2*pi*3e3*t);          % two-tone message, W = 3 kHz
fb = [0:N/2-1, -N/2:-1]*fs/N;                                       % FFT-bin frequencies
c = cos(2*pi*fc*t); sn = sin(2*pi*fc*t);
mh = hilbert_fft(m);
dsb = m.*c; usb = m.*c - mh.*sn; lsb = m.*c + mh.*sn;
H = min(max((abs(fb) - (fc - 1.5e3))/3e3, 0), 1);                  % VSB filter: H(fc-x)+H(fc+x) = 1
vsb = 2*real(ifft(fft(dsb).*H));
names = {'DSB-SC','USB','LSB','VSB'}; sigs = {dsb, usb, lsb, vsb};
fprintf('%8s %8s %22s %20s %6s\n','signal','power','occupied band (kHz)','recovered SNR (dB)','gain');
f2 = (-N/2:N/2-1)*fs/N;
for k = 1:4
    s = sigs{k}; S = abs(fftshift(fft(s)))/N; pos = f2 > 0 & S > 1e-3;
    y = lpf(2*s.*cos(2*pi*fc*t), 5e3, fs); g = (y*m')/(m*m'); e = y - g*m; q = 10*log10(sum((g*m).^2)/sum(e.^2));
    if q > 100, qs = '> 100 (exact)'; else, qs = sprintf('%.1f', q); end
    fprintf('%8s %8.4f %10.1f - %5.1f %20s %6.2f\n', names{k}, mean(s.^2), min(f2(pos))/1e3, max(f2(pos))/1e3, qs, g);
end
fprintf('\nPhase error in the coherent DSB-SC detector:\n');
for deg = [0 30 60 90]
    y = lpf(2*dsb.*cos(2*pi*fc*t + deg*pi/180), 5e3, fs); g = (y*m')/(m*m');
    fprintf('  phi = %2d deg: output gain = %6.3f  (cos phi = %.3f)\n', deg, g, cosd(deg));
end
figure('Position',[50 50 1100 600]);
for k = 1:4
    subplot(2,2,k); stem(f2/1e3, abs(fftshift(fft(sigs{k})))/N, 'Marker','none'); xlim([-26 26]); grid on; title([names{k} ': two-sided spectrum']); xlabel('f (kHz)');
end

function y = hilbert_fft(x)       % -90 deg phase shift at every frequency
    N = numel(x); f = [0:N/2-1, -N/2:-1]; y = real(ifft(fft(x).*(-1i*sign(f))));
end
function y = lpf(x, fcut, fs)      % ideal low-pass filter in the frequency domain
    N = numel(x); f = [0:N/2-1, -N/2:-1]*fs/N; X = fft(x); X(abs(f) > fcut) = 0; y = real(ifft(X));
end

Python · e3_envelope_detector.py numpy, matplotlib
"""E3  Diode envelope detector: choosing RC (ripple vs diagonal clipping), THD of the output.
Ideal-diode peak detector model. Requires: numpy, matplotlib."""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 4e6; T = 4e-3; t = np.arange(int(fs*T))/fs
fc, fm, mu, Ac = 200e3, 2e3, 0.6, 1.0
s = Ac*(1 + mu*np.cos(2*np.pi*fm*t))*np.cos(2*np.pi*fc*t)
RC_max = np.sqrt(1 - mu**2)/(mu*2*np.pi*fm)          # diagonal-clipping limit
print(f"1/fc = {1e6/fc:.1f} us,  RC_max = sqrt(1-mu^2)/(mu*wm) = {RC_max*1e6:.1f} us")

def detector(s, RC):
    """Ideal diode + RC: capacitor charges instantly to the input peak and discharges as exp(-t/RC)."""
    v = np.zeros_like(s); k = np.exp(-1/(fs*RC)); v[0] = s[0]
    for n in range(1, len(s)): v[n] = max(s[n], v[n-1]*k)
    return v

def thd(v):
    x = v[len(v)//2:]; x = x - x.mean(); X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x*np.hanning(len(x)))); f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1/fs)
    a = [X[np.argmin(abs(f - h*fm)) - 2: np.argmin(abs(f - h*fm)) + 3].max() for h in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)]
    rip = X[np.argmin(abs(f - fc)) - 3: np.argmin(abs(f - fc)) + 4].max()
    return 100*np.sqrt(sum(q*q for q in a[1:]))/a[0], 20*np.log10(rip/a[0])

print(f"{'RC (us)':>8s} {'THD (%)':>8s} {'ripple vs tone (dB)':>20s}  verdict")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(10, 7), sharex=True)
for i, RC in enumerate([10e-6, 80e-6, 300e-6]):
    v = detector(s, RC); d, r = thd(v)
    verdict = 'too much carrier ripple' if RC < 10/fc else ('diagonal clipping' if RC > RC_max else 'good')
    print(f"{RC*1e6:8.0f} {d:8.2f} {r:20.1f}  {verdict}")
    n = (t > 2e-3) & (t < 3e-3)
    ax[i].plot(t[n]*1e3, s[n], c='0.75', lw=0.5); ax[i].plot(t[n]*1e3, Ac*(1 + mu*np.cos(2*np.pi*fm*t[n])), 'k--', lw=1); ax[i].plot(t[n]*1e3, v[n], 'r', lw=1.4)
    ax[i].set(title=f'RC = {RC*1e6:.0f} µs: {verdict}', ylabel='V'); ax[i].grid(alpha=.4)
ax[-1].set_xlabel('t (ms)'); fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('e3_envelope_detector.png', dpi=110)
plt.show()
MATLAB · e3_envelope_detector.m no toolboxes; runs in Octave
% E3  Diode envelope detector: choosing RC (ripple vs diagonal clipping). Ideal diode + RC model. Core MATLAB.
clear; clc; close all;
fs = 4e6; T = 4e-3; t = (0:round(fs*T)-1)/fs;
fc = 200e3; fm = 2e3; mu = 0.6; Ac = 1;
s = Ac*(1 + mu*cos(2*pi*fm*t)).*cos(2*pi*fc*t);
RCmax = sqrt(1 - mu^2)/(mu*2*pi*fm);

fprintf('%8s %8s %20s  verdict\n','RC (us)','THD (%)','ripple vs tone (dB)');
RCs = [10e-6 80e-6 300e-6]; figure('Position',[50 50 1000 700]);
for i = 1:3
    RC = RCs(i); v = detector(s, RC, fs); [d, r] = thd_ripple(v, fs, fm, fc);
    if RC < 10/fc, verdict = 'too much carrier ripple'; elseif RC > RCmax, verdict = 'diagonal clipping'; else, verdict = 'good'; end
    fprintf('%8.0f %8.2f %20.1f  %s\n', RC*1e6, d, r, verdict);
    n = t > 2e-3 & t < 3e-3;
    subplot(3,1,i); plot(t(n)*1e3, s(n), 'Color', [.75 .75 .75]); hold on;
    plot(t(n)*1e3, Ac*(1 + mu*cos(2*pi*fm*t(n))), 'k--'); plot(t(n)*1e3, v(n), 'r', 'LineWidth', 1.4); grid on;
    title(sprintf('RC = %.0f us: %s', RC*1e6, verdict));
end

function v = detector(s, RC, fs)
    v = zeros(size(s)); k = exp(-1/(fs*RC)); v(1) = s(1);
    for n = 2:numel(s), v(n) = max(s(n), v(n-1)*k); end
end
function [d, r] = thd_ripple(v, fs, fm, fc)
    x = v(floor(end/2)+1:end); x = x - mean(x); L = numel(x);
    w = 0.5 - 0.5*cos(2*pi*(0:L-1)/(L-1)); X = abs(fft(x.*w)); X = X(1:floor(L/2)+1); f = (0:floor(L/2))*fs/L;
    a = zeros(1,5);
    for h = 1:5, [~, k] = min(abs(f - h*fm)); a(h) = max(X(k-2:k+2)); end
    [~, k] = min(abs(f - fc)); rip = max(X(k-3:k+3));
    d = 100*sqrt(sum(a(2:end).^2))/a(1); r = 20*log10(rip/a(1));
end

"""E4  Tone FM spectrum: Bessel coefficients, Carson's rule, carrier null, NBFM vs WBFM.
Requires: numpy, scipy (for jv), matplotlib."""
import numpy as np
from scipy.special import jv
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 400e3; T = 0.1; t = np.arange(int(fs*T))/fs        # 0.1 s -> 10 Hz resolution
fc, fm, Ac = 50e3, 1e3, 1.0

def fm_signal(beta):
    return Ac*np.cos(2*np.pi*fc*t + beta*np.sin(2*np.pi*fm*t))   # s(t) = Ac cos(wc t + beta sin wm t)

def lines(s):
    X = np.fft.fft(s)/len(s); f = np.fft.fftfreq(len(s), 1/fs)
    return lambda n: abs(X[np.argmin(abs(f - (fc + n*fm)))])*2       # one-sided line amplitude

print("beta   n:  measured |line|   theory |J_n(beta)|")
for beta in (0.2, 1.0, 2.405, 5.0):
    L = lines(fm_signal(beta))
    row = '  '.join(f"{n}:{L(n):.4f}/{abs(jv(n, beta)):.4f}" for n in range(0, 6))
    print(f"{beta:5.3f}  {row}")

print(f"\n{'beta':>6s} {'Carson B (kHz)':>15s} {'power in Carson':>16s} {'1% rule B (kHz)':>16s}")
for beta in (0.2, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0):
    nc = int(np.floor(beta + 1)); pin = jv(0, beta)**2 + 2*sum(jv(n, beta)**2 for n in range(1, nc + 1))
    n1 = max([n for n in range(0, 60) if abs(jv(n, beta)) >= 0.01] + [0])
    print(f"{beta:6.1f} {2*(beta + 1)*fm/1e3:15.1f} {100*pin:15.2f}% {2*n1*fm/1e3:16.1f}")
s = fm_signal(5.0); print(f"\nPower check (beta = 5): mean(s^2) = {np.mean(s**2):.4f}, Ac^2/2 = {Ac**2/2:.4f}")
print(f"Carrier null: J0(2.405) = {jv(0, 2.405):.5f} -> for fm = 1 kHz the carrier vanishes at delta f = 2.405 kHz")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 6.5))
for a, beta in zip(ax.flat, (0.2, 1.0, 2.405, 5.0)):
    s = fm_signal(beta); X = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft(s))/len(s); f = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fftfreq(len(s), 1/fs))
    k = np.abs(X) > 1e-3
    a.stem(f[k]/1e3, np.abs(X[k]), markerfmt=' ', basefmt=' ')
    B = 2*(beta + 1)*fm; a.axvspan((fc - B/2)/1e3, (fc + B/2)/1e3, alpha=.12, color='g'); a.axvspan((-fc - B/2)/1e3, (-fc + B/2)/1e3, alpha=.12, color='g')
    a.set(title=f'β = {beta}: two-sided spectrum (Carson band shaded)', xlabel='f (kHz)', xlim=(-60, 60)); a.grid(alpha=.4)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('e4_fm_spectrum.png', dpi=110)
plt.show()

"""E5  FM demodulation (I/Q discriminator), output SNR vs CNR (threshold), and de-emphasis.
Requires: numpy, matplotlib."""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

fs = 512e3; N = 2**18; t = np.arange(N)/fs          # 0.51 s
fm, df, W = 1e3, 5e3, 1.2e3                         # tone, deviation (beta = 5), output (audio) bandwidth W
m = np.cos(2*np.pi*fm*t)
phase = 2*np.pi*df*np.cumsum(m)/fs                   # 2*pi*kf * integral(m)
z = np.exp(1j*phase)                                 # complex baseband FM (carrier at 0 Hz), power 1
BT = 2*(df + fm)                                     # Carson bandwidth = 12 kHz

def bandlimit(x, f_lo, f_hi):
    X = np.fft.fft(x); f = np.fft.fftfreq(len(x), 1/fs); X[(f < f_lo) | (f > f_hi)] = 0; return np.fft.ifft(X)

def discriminator(r):
    return np.angle(r[1:]*np.conj(r[:-1]))*fs/(2*np.pi)   # instantaneous frequency (Hz)

def out_snr(y):
    y = np.real(bandlimit(y - y.mean(), -W, W)); ref = m[1:]
    g = np.dot(y, ref)/np.dot(ref, ref); e = y - g*ref
    return 10*np.log10(np.sum((g*ref)**2)/np.sum(e**2))

print(f"{'CNR in B_T (dB)':>16s} {'gamma (dB)':>11s} {'SNR_o meas (dB)':>16s} {'theory 3/2(df/W)^2 g':>21s}")
cnrs = np.arange(0, 31, 3); meas = []; theo = []
for cnr in cnrs:
    N0 = 1/(10**(cnr/10)*BT)                          # noise PSD so that P/(N0*BT) = CNR
    n = np.sqrt(N0*fs/2)*(rng.standard_normal(N) + 1j*rng.standard_normal(N))
    r = bandlimit(z + n, -BT/2, BT/2)                 # IF filter = Carson bandwidth
    y = discriminator(r)
    gamma = 1/(N0*W)                                  # baseband reference P/(N0 W)
    th = 10*np.log10(1.5*(df/W)**2*gamma)            # SNR_o = 3 (df/W)^2 P_m gamma, P_m = 1/2
    meas.append(out_snr(y)); theo.append(th)
    print(f"{cnr:16.0f} {10*np.log10(gamma):11.1f} {meas[-1]:16.1f} {th:21.1f}")

# de-emphasis improvement (theory) for broadcast parameters
for tau in (50e-6, 75e-6):
    f1 = 1/(2*np.pi*tau); r = 15e3/f1; I = r**3/(3*(r - np.arctan(r)))
    print(f"de-emphasis tau = {tau*1e6:.0f} us: f1 = {f1:.0f} Hz, improvement = {10*np.log10(I):.1f} dB (W = 15 kHz)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
ax[0].plot(cnrs, meas, 'o-', label='measured'); ax[0].plot(cnrs, theo, 'k--', label='3/2·(Δf/W)²·γ (above threshold)')
ax[0].axvline(10, c='r', ls=':', label='≈ threshold (10 dB)'); ax[0].set(xlabel='CNR in B_T (dB)', ylabel='output SNR (dB)', title='FM threshold effect (β = 5)'); ax[0].legend(); ax[0].grid(alpha=.4)
N0 = 1/(10**(6/10)*BT); r = bandlimit(z + np.sqrt(N0*fs/2)*(rng.standard_normal(N) + 1j*rng.standard_normal(N)), -BT/2, BT/2); y = discriminator(r)
n = slice(0, int(4e-3*fs)); ax[1].plot(t[1:][n]*1e3, y[n]/1e3, lw=.8); ax[1].plot(t[n]*1e3, df*m[n]/1e3, 'k--')
ax[1].set(xlabel='t (ms)', ylabel='inst. frequency (kHz)', title='CNR 6 dB: clicks (2π phase slips)'); ax[1].grid(alpha=.4)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('e5_fm_demod_noise.png', dpi=110)
plt.show()

end

    f1 = 1/(2*pi*tau); r = 15e3/f1; I = r^3/(3*(r - atan(r)));
    fprintf('de-emphasis tau = %.0f us: f1 = %.0f Hz, improvement = %.1f dB (W = 15 kHz)\n', tau*1e6, f1, 10*log10(I));
end

Python · e6_pm_vs_fm.py numpy, matplotlib
"""E6  PM vs FM: same message, deviation vs message frequency, PM demodulation by phase detection.
Requires: numpy, matplotlib."""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 400e3; t = np.arange(int(fs*0.02))/fs; fc = 20e3
kf, kp = 2e3, 1.0                                  # FM: 2 kHz/V,  PM: 1 rad/V

def mods(m):
    s_fm = np.cos(2*np.pi*fc*t + 2*np.pi*kf*np.cumsum(m)/fs)
    s_pm = np.cos(2*np.pi*fc*t + kp*m)
    return s_fm, s_pm

def inst_freq(s):
    """Instantaneous frequency from the analytic signal (FFT Hilbert)."""
    X = np.fft.fft(s); f = np.fft.fftfreq(len(s)); X[f < 0] = 0; X[f > 0] *= 2; z = np.fft.ifft(X)
    return np.diff(np.unwrap(np.angle(z)))*fs/(2*np.pi), z

print(f"{'fm (Hz)':>8s} {'FM: dev (Hz)':>13s} {'FM beta':>8s} {'FM Carson (kHz)':>16s} {'PM: dev (Hz)':>13s} {'PM beta':>8s} {'PM Carson (kHz)':>16s}")
for fm in (500, 1000, 2000, 4000):
    m = np.sin(2*np.pi*fm*t)
    sf, sp = mods(m); ff, _ = inst_freq(sf); fp, _ = inst_freq(sp); core = slice(2000, -2000)
    dfm = (ff[core].max() - ff[core].min())/2; dpm = (fp[core].max() - fp[core].min())/2
    print(f"{fm:8d} {dfm:13.0f} {dfm/fm:8.2f} {2*(dfm + fm)/1e3:16.1f} {dpm:13.0f} {dpm/fm:8.2f} {2*(dpm + fm)/1e3:16.1f}")
print("Theory: FM deviation = kf*Am = 2000 Hz (fixed);  PM deviation = kp*Am*fm (grows with fm), beta_PM = kp*Am = 1.")

# PM demodulation: phase of the analytic signal relative to the carrier
m = np.sin(2*np.pi*1000*t); _, sp = mods(m); _, z = inst_freq(sp)
ph = np.unwrap(np.angle(z*np.exp(-1j*2*np.pi*fc*t))); ph -= ph.mean()
core = slice(2000, -2000); g = np.dot(ph[core], m[core])/np.dot(m[core], m[core]); err = ph[core] - g*m[core]
print(f"PM demodulation: recovered gain = {g:.4f} rad/V (kp = {kp}), residual = {10*np.log10(np.mean(err**2)/np.mean((g*m[core])**2)):.1f} dB")

tri = lambda tt: 2*np.abs(2*((tt*500) % 1) - 1) - 1
fig, ax = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(10, 8), sharex=True)
m = tri(t); sf, sp = mods(m); ff, _ = inst_freq(sf); fp, _ = inst_freq(sp); n = slice(0, int(4e-3*fs))
ax[0].plot(t[n]*1e3, m[n]); ax[0].set(title='message: 500 Hz triangle')
ax[1].plot(t[n]*1e3, sf[n], lw=.6); ax[1].set(title='FM: frequency follows m(t)')
ax[2].plot(t[n]*1e3, sp[n], lw=.6, c='C3'); ax[2].set(title='PM: phase follows m(t)')
ax[3].plot(t[1:][n]*1e3, (ff[n] - fc)/1e3, label='FM'); ax[3].plot(t[1:][n]*1e3, (fp[n] - fc)/1e3, 'C3--', label='PM'); ax[3].set(title='instantaneous frequency − f_c (kHz)', xlabel='t (ms)'); ax[3].legend()
for a in ax: a.grid(alpha=.4)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('e6_pm_vs_fm.png', dpi=110)
plt.show()

ph = unwrap(angle(z.*exp(-1i*2*pi*fc*t))); ph = ph - mean(ph);
g = (ph(core)*m(core)')/(m(core)*m(core)');
fprintf('PM demodulation: recovered gain = %.4f rad/V (kp = %g)\n', g, kp);

function [fi, z] = inst_freq(s, fs)     % instantaneous frequency from the analytic signal
    N = numel(s); X = fft(s); h = zeros(1,N); h(1) = 1; h(2:N/2) = 2; h(N/2+1) = 1;
    z = ifft(X.*h); fi = diff(unwrap(angle(z)))*fs/(2*pi);
end

E7superhet

Expected output (Python and MATLAB agree)

Python · e7_superhet.py numpy, matplotlib
"""E7  Superheterodyne conversion: two AM stations, mixing to a 455 kHz IF, image frequency and the
benefit of an RF pre-selector. Frequencies are real broadcast values. Requires: numpy, matplotlib."""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 8e6; N = 2**16; t = np.arange(N)/fs            # 8.2 ms
fIF = 455e3
fd = 1000e3                                          # desired station 1000 kHz, 1 kHz tone
fim = fd + 2*fIF                                     # image = 1910 kHz (LO above)
fLO = fd + fIF                                       # 1455 kHz
desired = (1 + 0.5*np.cos(2*np.pi*1e3*t))*np.cos(2*np.pi*fd*t)
image = 1.0*(1 + 0.5*np.cos(2*np.pi*2.5e3*t))*np.cos(2*np.pi*fim*t)     # equally strong image station, 2.5 kHz tone

def bpf(x, f0, B):
    X = np.fft.fft(x); f = np.abs(np.fft.fftfreq(len(x), 1/fs)); X[np.abs(f - f0) > B/2] = 0; return np.real(np.fft.ifft(X))
def rf_tank(x, f0, Q):
    """Single-tuned RF pre-selector |H| = 1/sqrt(1 + Q^2 (f/f0 - f0/f)^2) applied in frequency domain."""
    X = np.fft.fft(x); f = np.abs(np.fft.fftfreq(len(x), 1/fs)) + 1e-9; H = 1/np.sqrt(1 + (Q*(f/f0 - f0/f))**2); return np.real(np.fft.ifft(X*H))
def tone_level(y, ft):
    y = y - y.mean(); Y = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(y*np.hanning(len(y)))); f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(y), 1/fs); k = np.argmin(abs(f - ft)); return Y[k-2:k+3].max()

lo = np.cos(2*np.pi*fLO*t)
print(f"f_RF = {fd/1e3:.0f} kHz, f_LO = {fLO/1e3:.0f} kHz, f_IF = {fIF/1e3:.0f} kHz, image = {fim/1e3:.0f} kHz")
for Q in (None, 20, 60):
    rf = desired + image if Q is None else rf_tank(desired + image, fd, Q)
    ifs = bpf(rf*lo, fIF, 10e3)                     # mixer + 10 kHz IF filter
    env = np.abs(ifs); env = bpf(env, 0, 10e3)       # crude envelope detector (rectify + LPF)
    a1, a2 = tone_level(env, 1e3), tone_level(env, 2.5e3)
    rej = 20*np.log10(a1/a2)
    th = '' if Q is None else f"(theory IFRR = {20*np.log10(np.sqrt(1 + (Q*(fim/fd - fd/fim))**2)):.1f} dB)"
    print(f"RF pre-selector Q = {str(Q):>4s}: desired 1 kHz tone vs image 2.5 kHz tone at the output = {rej:6.1f} dB {th}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 6))
for a, (x, title) in zip(ax, ((desired + image, 'antenna: desired 1000 kHz + image 1910 kHz'), (bpf((desired + image)*lo, fIF, 10e3), 'after mixer + IF filter (no pre-selector): both land on 455 kHz'))):
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x))/len(x)*2; f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1/fs)
    a.plot(f/1e3, 20*np.log10(X + 1e-6)); a.set(xlim=(0, 2500), ylim=(-80, 5), title=title, xlabel='f (kHz)', ylabel='dB'); a.grid(alpha=.4)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('e7_superhet.png', dpi=110)
plt.show()
MATLAB · e7_superhet.m no toolboxes; runs in Octave
% E7  Superheterodyne conversion: desired 1000 kHz + image 1910 kHz, IF 455 kHz, RF pre-selector Q. Core MATLAB.
clear; clc; close all;
fs = 8e6; N = 2^16; t = (0:N-1)/fs;
fIF = 455e3; fd = 1000e3; fim = fd + 2*fIF; fLO = fd + fIF;
desired = (1 + 0.5*cos(2*pi*1e3*t)).*cos(2*pi*fd*t);
image = (1 + 0.5*cos(2*pi*2.5e3*t)).*cos(2*pi*fim*t);
lo = cos(2*pi*fLO*t);
fprintf('f_RF = %.0f kHz, f_LO = %.0f kHz, f_IF = %.0f kHz, image = %.0f kHz\n', fd/1e3, fLO/1e3, fIF/1e3, fim/1e3);
for Q = [0 20 60]
    x = desired + image; if Q > 0, x = rf_tank(x, fd, Q, fs); end
    ifs = bpf(x.*lo, fIF, 10e3, fs); env = bpf(abs(ifs), 0, 10e3, fs);
    rej = 20*log10(tone_level(env, 1e3, fs)/tone_level(env, 2.5e3, fs));
    if Q == 0, fprintf('no pre-selector: desired vs image tone at output = %6.1f dB\n', rej);
    else, fprintf('RF pre-selector Q = %2d: desired vs image = %6.1f dB (theory IFRR = %.1f dB)\n', Q, rej, 20*log10(sqrt(1 + (Q*(fim/fd - fd/fim))^2))); end
end

function y = bpf(x, f0, B, fs)
    N = numel(x); f = abs([0:N/2-1, -N/2:-1]*fs/N); X = fft(x); X(abs(f - f0) > B/2) = 0; y = real(ifft(X));
end
function y = rf_tank(x, f0, Q, fs)
    N = numel(x); f = abs([0:N/2-1, -N/2:-1]*fs/N) + 1e-9; H = 1./sqrt(1 + (Q*(f/f0 - f0./f)).^2); y = real(ifft(fft(x).*H));
end
function a = tone_level(y, ft, fs)
    y = y - mean(y); L = numel(y); w = 0.5 - 0.5*cos(2*pi*(0:L-1)/(L-1)); Y = abs(fft(y.*w)); Y = Y(1:L/2+1);
    f = (0:L/2)*fs/L; [~, k] = min(abs(f - ft)); a = max(Y(k-2:k+2));
end

Python · e8_pll.py numpy, matplotlib
"""E8  Phase-locked loop: acquisition of a frequency step and demodulation of FM (discrete-time model of an
analog second-order PLL with a proportional-plus-integral loop filter). Requires: numpy, matplotlib."""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 200e3; T = 0.03; N = int(fs*T); t = np.arange(N)/fs
f0 = 10e3                                   # VCO free-running frequency
Kd, kv = 1.0, 5e3                           # phase-detector gain (V/rad), VCO gain (Hz/V)
zeta, fn = 0.707, 2000.0                     # damping and natural frequency of the loop
wn = 2*np.pi*fn; K = 2*np.pi*kv*Kd
kp_, ki_ = 2*zeta*wn/K, wn**2/K             # PI loop filter gains so that the loop has (zeta, wn)
print(f"Loop: Kd = {Kd} V/rad, kv = {kv/1e3} kHz/V, zeta = {zeta}, fn = {fn} Hz -> Kp = {kp_:.4f}, Ki = {ki_:.2f}")

def run(fin):
    th_in = 2*np.pi*np.cumsum(fin)/fs
    th_v = 0.0; integ = 0.0; v = np.zeros(N); err = np.zeros(N)
    for n in range(N):
        e = Kd*np.sin(th_in[n] - th_v)          # multiplier-type phase detector (low-pass part)
        integ += ki_*e/fs; v[n] = kp_*e + integ  # PI loop filter
        th_v += 2*np.pi*(f0 + kv*v[n])/fs        # VCO
        err[n] = e
    return v, err

# 1) frequency step of +1 kHz at 5 ms
fin = f0 + 1e3*(t >= 5e-3); v, err = run(fin)
print(f"Frequency step +1 kHz: final control voltage = {v[-1]:.4f} V (expected 1000/kv = {1e3/kv:.4f} V); final phase error = {np.degrees(np.arcsin(err[-1])):.3f} deg")
k = np.where(np.abs(v - 0.2) > 0.02*0.2)[0]; ts = (t[k[-1]] - 5e-3)*1e3 if len(k) else 0
print(f"2 % settling time ≈ {ts:.2f} ms (theory ≈ 4/(zeta*wn) = {4/(zeta*wn)*1e3:.2f} ms)")
# 2) FM demodulation: 200 Hz tone, 1.5 kHz deviation
m = np.cos(2*np.pi*200*t); fin2 = f0 + 1.5e3*m; v2, _ = run(fin2)
core = t > 10e-3; g = np.dot(v2[core], m[core])/np.dot(m[core], m[core])
print(f"FM demodulation: v(t) = {g:.4f}·m(t) (theory kf/kv = 1500/5000 = 0.3000)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 6))
ax[0].plot(t*1e3, v, label='VCO control v(t)'); ax[0].axhline(0.2, c='k', ls='--', lw=.8); ax[0].set(title='PLL response to a +1 kHz input frequency step', xlabel='ms', ylabel='V'); ax[0].legend()
ax[1].plot(t*1e3, v2, label='PLL output v(t)'); ax[1].plot(t*1e3, 0.3*m, 'k--', label='(k_f/k_v)·m(t)'); ax[1].set(title='PLL as FM demodulator', xlabel='ms', ylabel='V'); ax[1].legend()
for a in ax: a.grid(alpha=.4)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('e8_pll.png', dpi=110)
plt.show()
MATLAB · e8_pll.m no toolboxes; runs in Octave
% E8  Phase-locked loop: frequency-step acquisition and FM demodulation (2nd-order loop, PI filter). Core MATLAB.
clear; clc; close all;
fs = 200e3; T = 0.03; N = round(fs*T); t = (0:N-1)/fs;
f0 = 10e3; Kd = 1; kv = 5e3; zeta = 0.707; fn = 2000;
wn = 2*pi*fn; K = 2*pi*kv*Kd; Kp = 2*zeta*wn/K; Ki = wn^2/K;
fprintf('Loop: Kd = %g V/rad, kv = %g kHz/V, zeta = %g, fn = %g Hz -> Kp = %.4f, Ki = %.2f\n', Kd, kv/1e3, zeta, fn, Kp, Ki);
fin = f0 + 1e3*(t >= 5e-3); [v, err] = pll(fin, fs, f0, Kd, kv, Kp, Ki);
fprintf('Frequency step +1 kHz: final control voltage = %.4f V (expected %.4f V)\n', v(end), 1e3/kv);
k = find(abs(v - 0.2) > 0.02*0.2, 1, 'last'); fprintf('2%% settling time = %.2f ms (theory ~ 4/(zeta*wn) = %.2f ms)\n', (t(k) - 5e-3)*1e3, 4/(zeta*wn)*1e3);
m = cos(2*pi*200*t); [v2, ~] = pll(f0 + 1.5e3*m, fs, f0, Kd, kv, Kp, Ki);
c = t > 10e-3; g = (v2(c)*m(c)')/(m(c)*m(c)');
fprintf('FM demodulation: v(t) = %.4f m(t) (theory kf/kv = %.4f)\n', g, 1.5e3/kv);
figure; subplot(2,1,1); plot(t*1e3, v); grid on; title('PLL response to a +1 kHz frequency step'); xlabel('ms');
subplot(2,1,2); plot(t*1e3, v2, t*1e3, 0.3*m, 'k--'); grid on; title('PLL as FM demodulator'); xlabel('ms');

function [v, err] = pll(fin, fs, f0, Kd, kv, Kp, Ki)
    N = numel(fin); th_in = 2*pi*cumsum(fin)/fs; th_v = 0; integ = 0; v = zeros(1,N); err = v;
    for n = 1:N
        e = Kd*sin(th_in(n) - th_v); integ = integ + Ki*e/fs; v(n) = Kp*e + integ;
        th_v = th_v + 2*pi*(f0 + kv*v(n))/fs; err(n) = e;
    end
end
